subtopic: DROUGHT CONDITIONS IN WEST-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: DROUGHT CONDITIONS IN WEST-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Before the orders of the day are called, Mr. Speaker, I ask leave to move the adjournment of the house under standing order 26 for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely the drought conditions prevailing in western Canada which threaten an imminent collapse of cattle prices and farm income.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: DROUGHT CONDITIONS IN WEST-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: I think it is unnecessary to hear any argument on this question. It seems to me that it is a matter which could very readily be debated in the budget debate which continues today. The requirement of urgency of debate therefore is hardly satisfied. I accept the proposition that this is an urgent and important public matter to which the Leader of the Opposition draws attention. It is a definite matter of public importance. However, that is not the criterion in determining whether standing order 26 should be applied. The criterion is whether there is an opportunity to debate this matter in an effective way.

subtopic: DROUGHT CONDITIONS IN WEST-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Before you make your decision, Mr. Speaker, perhaps I may be permitted to explain that, as you have stated, this is a matter of urgency; it is not only a matter of urgency of debate but a matter of urgency of action on the part of the government to deal with a situation which is so serious and is becoming worse every day and which, across the border in the United States, has resulted in five states being declared disaster areas.

subtopic: DROUGHT CONDITIONS IN WEST-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: DROUGHT CONDITIONS IN WEST-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: The urgency of debate-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: DROUGHT CONDITIONS IN WEST-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: If the hon. member wishes to say anything about urgency of debate I will hear him, but not on the issue, because that matter can be debated.

subtopic: DROUGHT CONDITIONS IN WEST-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Urgency of debate I should think would be required, Mr. Speaker, so we can ask the government at once to tell us what action they propose to take in regard to the collapse of cattle prices because of lack of fodder, and in regard to the necessity of doing something about this matter and the decline of farm income generally in the face of this situation. It is quite true that in the budget debate we can deal with these matters, but a special debate would give to the government the opportunity of telling us at once what plans the government have to deal with this situation which is now so very serious.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: DROUGHT CONDITIONS IN WEST-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
In view of the statements made by the hon. member, Mr. Speaker, I think I should point out first that the opportunity is available to discuss this matter today. There is no necessity for any adjournment of the house because the government has acted already, has given consideration to that matter, has already received representations from the province of Manitoba and will receive representations from the province of Saskatchewan if they have not come to hand this morning. Every assistance is going to be provided in connection with the provision of fodder and also the transfer of cattle from non-fodder areas to fodder areas.
In so far as the reference to the United States is concerned may I say this. We have been in touch with the government of the United States, our purpose being to secure from the United States permission to have those areas that have been put in grazing or in hay under the soil bank available to us in

Inquiries of the Ministry Canada for the cutting of the hay. The United States, in view of the circumstances in which it finds itself in the northern states, is giving consideration to that request but I do not look hopefully in that direction. Action has been taken already.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: DROUGHT CONDITIONS IN WEST-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: I think the matter might be pursued by a question on the orders of the day if hon. members so desire, but I am not satisfied that there is not ample opportunity to put before the house and the government all the considerations that apply to this important matter in the debate which will follow immediately after the calling of the orders of the day. speechtext: -but may I ask the Prime Minister again what action he is taking to prevent the collapse of prices in the prairies, and what steps he has taken, if any, for freight assistance to transfer cattle from the prairie provinces to the east, where feed is available. Perhaps he will try to answer that one.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ESTABLISHMENT OF FLOOR PRICE
speechtext:
That is a matter for information, and I will give it. I was giving the information; the hon. gentleman did not have it. The committee of the privy council have given consideration to this matter and an order in council has been passed which in


effect is as follows. Due to drought conditions the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta face a very serious shortage of fodder for livestock and there has already been considerable distress in various areas of the west. To avoid a heavy liquidation of livestock, extraordinary measures will be necessary to provide fodder to drought areas and to move cattle from those areas to other areas for summer grazing.
The provinces of Manitoba and Saskatchewan are now formulating policies to bear part of the freight costs of bringing fodder to and moving cattle from drought areas, and have requested that the federal government share equally with the provinces the cost of such assistance. I think a similar request will also come from the province of Alberta.
As the house knows, similar assistance was provided to the provinces of Saskatchewan and Manitoba in 1958 due to drought conditions, and to all three prairie provinces in 1959 due to the loss of fodder from early snows. Therefore authorization has been given for the payment to the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta of one half of the amounts paid by these provinces for their transportation costs on shipments of fodder, for the movement of cattle to feed, and for the transportation of haying equipment from June 26 this year to March 31, 1962, subject of course to such terms and provisions as may be prescribed by the Minister of Agriculture.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The house resumed, from Friday, June 23, consideration of the motion of Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Benidickson. (Translation):

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was particularly impressed by the speech made last Tuesday by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming). The duty he was faced with then was most tricky, difficult and consequential.
Any budgetary measure has repercussions on the economy of a country, on its trade, its industry and its relations with other countries. One can imagine the tact, the knowhow and the knowledge required to perform such a task. The Minister of Finance proved once again last Tuesday that he possesses all those qualities to a great degree, and all members of the house should be unanimous in commending him in spite of the differences of opinion they might have.
I should also like to emphasize the courtesy he showed us, his French-speaking fellow citizens. Ever since his first budget speech, he has made it a point to express himself in our language to summarize some fundamental proposals. Since then, he has always been true to that line of conduct. I wish to congratulate him and to thank him. That means that he recognizes the important role his compatriots of French language and culture are

The Budget-Mr. Dorian called upon to play with their fellow citizens of English language and culture, in the economic life of our country. A reminder of this basic truth can only bring the two great people who founded this confederation of ours to work more closely and more efficiently together.
I have read with mixed feelings the speeches which were made concerning that most important document which was laid down by the Minister of Finance. A few of them were meaty and contained specific suggestions but, unfortunately, many of them seemed to go astray into the doubtful avenues of demagogy. However, if there is a debate that ought to be kept far and above all partisan or petty considerations, it is surely this one, because what is at stake in this instance is all the more serious as it involves our nation's economic progress and well-being. Faced with such a problem, it seems to me that we should proceed by the straightforward and enlightened ways of good sense, logic and objectivity in seeking the solutions called for by circumstances.
In order to fully understand the nature and the full weight of this budget, we should judge it on its substance and in the light of the facts and events of which it is but a result. It matters little whether the December estimates have met with adverse winds and have thus been in part invalidated by conditions for which surely the Minister of Finance cannot be held responsible. Under our system of government, where planned economy cannot be the rule and where economic activities are generally left to private enterprise, we have no cause to be shocked at this juncture. The government's role is limited to seeking and submitting measures which, in the present circumstances, seem most appropriate for stimulating this nation's economy and giving it such impulse that will carry it forward toward new achievements. There you have considered in its true perspective, the problem related to the budget and facing us as well as the Canadian people as a whole.
The measures introduced by the Minister of Finance have not been brought about in a haphazard way. Quite the contrary, they are part and parcel of a policy laid down previously, a policy which dominates those measures and a prerequisite of which is the economic independence of the nation.
They go back to the actions first taken by this government since coming into power and they are in line with the task assumed by the Conservative party, which is to throw off the yoke of foreign domination, under which we were gradually sinking.
As early as December 1960, the Minister of Finance had laid the necessary and logical
[Mr. Dorion.l

basis in his little budget which was a sort of prelude to the one which is now submitted to us. Both are based on the same spirit and have the same purposes. A brief summary will confirm this.
Most of the measures advocated by the Minister of Finance last December fall into three main groups-an increase and a channelling of national savings invested in Canada, an increase of income tax on revenues transferred abroad; and, finally, a review of the customs tariff.
The purpose of the first group of measures is to bring investment companies and pension funds to invest most of their money in Canada. In accordance with this, new industries in depressed areas that undertake to use local raw materials which have so far been exported and manufacturers of products which until now have been imported from abroad are entitled to double depreciation for one year.
In his budget speech, the minister stressed the interest with which this action was received by some industries. It looks as though we might expect good results in the field of employment and industrial development.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, surely I am not in a position to give more information than the Minister of Finance himself.
The second category of measures provided for an increase from 5 to 15 per cent of the

tax now levied by the government on income earned in Canada and transferred abroad. There is no question, under that legislation, of simply ballyragging foreign interests, but rather of ensuring that those interests contribute more to public expenses, and that the entry of foreign capital be limited to proportions more in line with the requirements of our economic independence.
On the other hand, and in order to encourage our own investments, the surtax of 4 per cent on the dividends of Canadian investments was abolished.
The third category of measures provided for the revision of some items of the customs tariff, and for the redefinition of products of a type made in Canada.
That redefinition, as wrote Mr. Jacques Parizeau, Montreal economist and professor at the Ecole des Hautes Etudes, in Montreal:
-is probably the most important aspect in the budget.
That was also the opinion of some particularly experienced businessmen. That measure could facilitate the working of anti-dumping legislation and at the same time protect our own manufactured products against certain imports which, by evading the intent of the law while observing its letter, can take advantage of the lower tariffs.
Other measures were also proposed such as the establishment of an export financing bank to help our industry to increase its sales abroad, in order to stimulate production and employment in this country.
Again, according to Mr. Jacques Parizeau, that December budget.
-is probably an outstanding event in the history of Canadian economic policy.
Another economist, Mr. Roland Parenteau, also professor at the Ecole des Hautes Etudes in Montreal, then expressed his views as follows:
Inasmuch as we are faced with a structural crisis, the nature of those various measures may turn the tide in the right direction. Already, the exchange rate has moved in a direction favourable to our trade balance. That alone might do more towards a permanent eradication of unemployment than all conceivable public works.
In his annual report to the shareholders of the Montreal city and district savings bank, Mr. Guy Vanier, chairman of the institution, also commended the Minister of Finance for setting the country in the right direction. Here is what he had to say:
Processing firms, provided they can count on a steady domestic market and on proper foreign trade possibilities, could, more than anything else, reduce unemployment in a progressive and permanent way.
The Budget-Mr. Dorion
Those are eloquent marks of appreciation resulting from an objective and unbiased study and which are certainly just as good as any criticism heard in this house. Being of immediate and long term significance, this budget encourages the growth of Canadian enterprise while reducing at the same time the benefits of foreign investors in Canada. Well, it is with that logical system that this budget was prepared as it is with that logical system that the various policies of this government have been pursued since the people of Canada gave us the responsibilities of power.
Like last December's budget, one of the main purposes of this one is to check foreign capital inflow into Canada while promoting Canadian investment in our own business.
Have we often stopped to think that since 1950, U.S. investments alone in Canadian business have reached over $3 billion, half of which have been invested in the oil industry? Should this government not be concerned and not increase the steps it had already taken to ensure Canadian economic independence?
As a second aim, we want to balance orn foreign trade as much as possible. International trade is a two-way road, but if the incoming road is wide and spacious while the outgoing one is narrow and difficult, it creates an unbalance which eventually bears heavily on the Canadian economy. The result for us is a weakening congestion of our manufacturing industry and a consequent increase in unemployment.
The government's present policy is in fact reversing the trend. In 1960, our exports rose by $225 million, or 5 per cent over the previous year, reaching a total of $5,395,300,000; our imports, with a drop of 2.1 per cent in relation to the previous year, totalled $5,495,800,000, leaving a total deficit of $100,500,000, as compared to a deficit of $368 million in 1959.
Some have been shocked at our budget deficit. However, should our international deficit not be our first concern? Should we not give top priority to a better balance in our external trade, and to the balance of payments, and try to maintain our main industries and to increase their production and manpower?
On this last point, I should like to point out the tariff amendments which are provided to ensure greater protection to some sections of the textile industry. I have been reading the complaints of the hon. member for Drum-mond-Arthabaska (Mr. Boulanger) in that regard, and his bitter words to the government and to Quebec members on the government side.
7114	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Dorion
Apparently the hon. member is totally unaware of the origin and nature of the problem, because otherwise, he would have kept cautiously silent or would have directed his complaints to his friends in the opposition.
Instead of reproaching others for their silence, he should have made a serious study of the problem and come up with specific proposals to solve it, proposals which his friends in the opposition would have been prepared to support.
First of all, I will remind him that it was the Bennett government which, through the 1932 Ottawa agreements, first afforded adequate protection for the textile industry. The measures then adopted in that field produced such results that according to economists that industry was one of those which suffered the least from the depression which affected most areas of the Canadian economy, a depression that did not originate with the Bennett administration, as some are wont to say, but with the financial crash of 1929, which occurred when the Liberal party was still in office. Following the return to power of the Liberals in 1935, the textile industry started on a downgrade. Since 1939, under their rule, specific duties protecting it have only been reduced. That is how the friends of the hon. member for Drummond-Artha-baska cared about an industry which in the province of Quebec, apart from the city of Montreal, involves at least one seventh of the labour force.
In that field as in many others, we had to endeavour to right the wrong that had been done, while complying with the international agreements binding our country. Therefore, as soon as he was sworn in, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) invited the tariff board to undertake a complete review of all GATT items regarding textiles, clothing and their manufacture. He gave them very definite instructions that in their recommendations they seriously take into account the economic situation of our own textile industries. In June 1958, the first findings were released and later on the minister hastened to order an increase in the tariffs on woollens subject to the British preferential rates.
What was the reaction of the leader and the friends of the hon. member for Drum-mond-Arthabaska? I would ask him to read again the speeches made in this house on August 13, 1958, particularly the one delivered by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) and the one, even more peremptory, delivered

by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill). If I had time, I would quote extensive extracts from that speech. But I will be content with reading the two paragraphs which in my opinion are the most characteristic:
(Text):
It is rather difficult to think of any industry that is much less indigenous. The raw material comes from abroad; the machinery in the plants comes from abroad, and the skills originally came from abroad. It is certainly not by any stretch of the imagination an indigenous industry.
What is being proposed, if it is seriously intended and if the government gets away with it this time, is to provide really high protection and really to make us self-sufficient in woollens at the expense of other Canadians. If that is so I would say we are embarking upon a most dangerous course. We should know now whether we are embarking on that course. It does not matter whether you look at this from the point of view of the generality of Canadian consumers or from the point of view of those particular industries that depend upon markets abroad-the United Kingdom, Italy and Japan are the three principal exporters to us at the present time of woollen goods-it seems to me that this policy is folly. It is contrary to our interests.
(Translation):
There you have the off-hand way in which the hon. member dealt with that industry set up in Sherbrooke in 1844, which numbers more than 800 plants throughout the country and which provides employment for about 70,000 people in the province of Quebec alone. In other words, that meant that if that industry could not subsist without protection, there was only one thing to do, and that was to drop it. Previously, he had made the following remarks:
(Text):
I consider that to increase the tariff on wool against the British is a very bad thing in itself. I will say something more about that, though I cannot add much to what was said so admirably by the Leader of the Opposition on that point. But I say this is just part of the policy; this is just the prelude to an increase in the most favoured nation rate against a country which is an essential market for our primary producers. The only excuse the tariff board could find was that this industry had social significance.
(Translation):
What does this mean? Would that reason not be sufficient? Are social consequences really such a poor excuse to the introduction of legislation? Since when does the concern for social classes or some of them not form part of the considerations that should command the attention of legislators?
Most fortunately, this government considers its obligations in a very different light. In view of the difficulties facing the textile industry, the government started negotiations

with countries enjoying the most favoured nation tariff. On April 10, 1959, an agreement was reached under which the tariff on woollens with those countries was increased proportionally to the increase in the preferential tariff. On May 31, 1960, the tariff board submitted further recommendations of which the most important, on that occasion, referred to coloured cotton goods. Through further agreements involving on our part concessions in other fields than the textile industry, and without the industry in general being adversely affected, tariff rates were increased.
A lot could also be said about the negotiations which the Canadian government has successfully conducted with Japan. Suffice it to recall that on May 5, 1960, the association of Canadian clothing and textile manufacturers commended the government for having, and I quote:
-tried to restore order and logic in our market which was upset by Japanese exportations.
And the president of the association, Mr. Peters, added:
Had it not been for the determination shown by the Canadian government in its discussions with the Japanese authorities these last months, the dangerous inflow would have been devastating.
Just a few weeks ago, the house was told by the Minister of Finance that Japan had consented to new voluntary quotas for the year 1961.
The present proposals of the Minister of Finance concerning textiles are pursuant to the logic of this policy. It is not surprising therefore that these last days, Mr. G. B. Gordon, president of Dominion Textile, stated that he was hopeful because of the firm intention of the Minister of Finance to avoid resorting to the most rigid forms of GATT during tariff renegotiations.
True to the imperatives which inspired the budget he brought down in December, which was aimed at reducing the flow of foreign capital to Canada and at encouraging Canadians to invest in their own country, the minister has also proposed a certain number of monetary policies which have already had an effect on business. The reduction of the interest rates will stop Canadian borrowing on foreign money markets and will stem the tide of imported capital. His task will be all the easier since the federal government will strive to put as little pressure as possible on the bond market.
The Budget-Mr. Dorion
To achieve that end, the government will finance its operations through short term credit and leave the whole long term bond market to municipalities, provinces and private enterprise. In that same frame of mind, the bonds which constitute the reserve of the unemployment insurance fund and are negotiable at any time will be replaced by nonnegotiable bonds. Moreover, to free the market, a government bond redemption fund will be created with a capital of $100 million, which will enable the buying of government bonds on the open market. Finally, the funds of the industrial development bank will be increased from $160 million to $400 million. Financing means available to our business firms will be increased accordingly.
It is with a feeling of relief that all those measures and others of a similar nature have been received throughout Canada. Among a great number of views expressed by both labour and business there is one which seems to summarize them all and which I would like to quote. It was expressed by Mr. F. D. Mathers, president of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association:
Of particular significance are the measures aimed at the devaluation of the Canadian dollar, as well as those reducing interest rates. The abolition of the excise tax on new automobiles and the tariff changes announced should help the industries concerned. Those items in the budget as well as the broadening of the industrial development bank's field of operations, the increased allowances for capital depreciation and for expenditures relating to scientific research, represent so many encouraging factors which, within the budget, should have a beneficial effect on employment opportunities.
In the establishment of the economic policy, the government's contribution must first of all be of a supplementary nature. It consists in promoting the co-ordination of efforts and in providing the community with general and specific means likely to make private enterprise more productive. To meet this requirement the present budget includes both fiscal and monetary measures. In the government's pursuit of policies leading to economic recovery, both types of measures are as related to one another as a pendulum to a clock. That is why obstacles had to be removed. I am confident that thanks to the hope which the minister's budget has given to the Canadian people, to the combined efforts of labour, business and finance, to that spirit of industry, co-operation and mutual help which prevails within the Canadian community, he will achieve the happy results we expect and will largely contribute to restore the economic independence of our country.

The Budget-Mr. Robichaud

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
For the
last 30 minutes we have listened to the Secretary of State trying to prove to this house that on March 30 of last year the Minister of Finance introduced a budget forecasting a surplus of $12 million and that on December 20 this forecast resulted in a further baby budget forecasting a deficit of $286 million, which has resulted on March 31 of this year in a net deficit of $353 million.
I feel it has taken a long time for the hon. gentleman to extend all his congratulations to the Minister of Finance. However, it now appears obvious that the members of the mutual admiration society have settled their strike after having been instructed by the dictatorial head of the government to keep


mum during the last two days of discussion of this budget. They have finally realized that such an attitude is not good for the proper conduct of parliamentary debate and not in the interests of the country. Probably this morning someone has brought to their attention an article which appeared in today's Globe and Mail entitled "Parliament's Business". I wish to put on record one paragraph of this article, which reads as follows:
It would be a mistake, for example, to attempt to cut short the current debate on the budget. Finance Minister Donald Fleming's proposals are among the most important business to come before this parliament and neither the government nor the opposition parties should attempt to stifle reasonable expression of opinion from the back benches.
As I have said, it now appears that this article has had some effect on the government side, because it now seems obvious that they intend to participate in the debate on this budget.
In introducing his budget on March 31, 1960 the Minister of Finance stated, as reported on page 2670 of Hansard:
Last year we emerged from a recession which has been caused by a number of factors.
Here we are on June 27, 1961, 14 months later, and according to the minister's present budget which is now under discussion we are still emerging from the recession. The Minister of Finance was not the only member of the cabinet who expressed similar views. Two months previously, as reported on page 517 of Hansard on January 29, 1960, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) said this in the house:
What about the recession? Everybody knows the recession is over. Everybody, that is, except hon. members opposite, particularly the hon. member for Essex East and his group.
Only one month later, on February 17, as reported at page 1164 of Hansard, the Minister of Public Works had this to say:
Although heavy government expenditure and government deficits are appropriate in times of recession I think we will all agree that in normal circumstances government expenditures should be limited to our income.
Now, every member of this house recalls the presentation of the budget on March 31, 1960. Every member of this house recalls the applause and desk thumping by supporters of the Minister of Finance when he announced that with revenue estimated at $5,892 million and expenditures at $5,880 million, he expected a surplus of $12 million for the coming year. It was on that occasion that the Minister of Finance said he was confident that employment would increase as the coming of spring opened up new job opportunities and as the economy, to use his words, continued its upward trend. As we on this side of the house said at the time, the only cure in the mind

of the Minister of Finance was to hope that unemployment would disappear with the melting of the snow. As the snow disappeared unemployment decreased to some extent, but within two or three months it had increased again to a record high and has remained at that level since. In fact the last report made public by the dominion bureau of statistics indicates that at the end of May of this year unemployment in Canada was 30,000 higher than it was at the same date last year.
I suggest we have here a government of confusion which has refused for two or three years to admit that there was a recession; a government which refused to admit that there was unusual and abnormal unemployment in this country. This is the government which refused to recognize the recession but which told us two years later that the recession was over and that we were then emerging from it.
Let us see what the Minister of Finance had to say about the government's tax policy at the time he introduced his budget on March 31, 1960. As reported at page 2681 of Hansard for that date the Minister of Finance is recorded as follows:
The fiscal policies we followed during our first year in office had a major influence in reducing both the depth and the duration of the recession, and by the third quarter of 1958 the low point of the recession had been passed and the forces of expansion began to gather momentum. By the spring of 1959 recovery was well on the way, and in my budget speech a year ago I recommended to this house policies which were designed to bring us back to a position of budgetary balance as soon as the economy had recovered the losses of the recession and was moving firmly forward and upward to new record achievements in production, employment and investment.
The minister then carried on to say:
The position we have now reached, with its sound prospect of a fully balanced budget,-
He insisted upon having a fully balanced budget. Then to continue his statement:
-represents the fruits of carefully designed policies carried forward over the past 18 months. This is not something that has just happened. It is the result of considered aims and efforts. It began with the great conversion loan of the summer of 1958 which made possible a policy of sound debt management which in turn restored public confidence in government credit and in our determination to control the powerful forces of inflation. It was continued in the expenditure controls and the tax changes of 1959, and is reinforced in this year's program of reduced controllable expenditures balanced by the continued promotion of constructive national development.
I ask what have been the results and what have been the fruits of these supposedly carefully designed policies carried forward by the present government over the past 18 months. The policies of the present government were so carefully designed and put forward that within nine months the Minister 90205-6-450
The Budget-Mr. Robichaud of Finance had to introduce in this house the baby budget of December 20, 1960. As a result of the supposedly carefully designed policies of the government the $12 million surplus of March 31 had been dissipated and in the minister's misconception there was born a new baby, a forecast deficit of $286 million. Furthermore we learn now, five months later, that this second forecast of the Minister of Finance has been wrong again, and from these carefully designed policies of the government the deficit is now increased to $353 million. In other words the December 20 baby has grown by another $77 million in a period of less than six months.
That was the result of the carefully designed policies of the present government; policies under which the debt of this country has increased by over $1,500 million in the last four years; policies under which unemployment in this country has reached a record high comparable only to that period of the hungry thirties when again there was a period of Conservative government. I ask, has this country ever before in its history seen more confusion, lack of policy or lack of leadership than it has from this government?
This is the government which, in 1957, told the people of this country that every Canadian man, woman and child was having his or her pocket picked by $30, and that every Canadian family was overtaxed by $120. This is the government which told the people of this country that it was time to take the unrepentant tax masters off the backs of the Canadian people. Those words were repeated throughout the campaign again and again by the Prime Minister.
Mr. Speaker, I ask what has been the fiscal record of this government since it took office in June, 1957. The record is as follows. In 1958 there was a deficit of $38 million; in 1959, a deficit of $609 million; in 1960, a deficit of $413 million; in 1961, a deficit of $300 million; an estimated deficit for the current fiscal year of $650 million, and there are clear indications now that it will likely be much higher than that. There has been deficit after deficit.
Notwithstanding these deficits the present government by its carefully designed policy has, in the last four years, dissipated a fund of $900 million which was reserved for unemployment insurance to protect the labour class of this country. In other words the record of this government-a blue government, always in the red-is that in the last four years it has added some $750 to every Canadian taxpayer's load. That is the government which, after its first year in office, blamed the situation on an administration which had left it with a $500 million surplus and a fund for unemployment insurance of
7118	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Robichaud over $900 million, with an average 3 per cent to 3 J per cent unemployment average in this country. This is the government which, as I said earlier, through statements made in this house by its Minister ol Labour and its Minister of Public Works, made it clear over 18 months ago that the recession in this country was over. These statements were confirmed in no uncertain terms, as I have shown, by the Minister of Finance in the presentation of his budget of March 31, 1960.
In introducing the present budget last week the Minister of Finance said, as reported at page 6642 of Hansard of June 20, 1961:
When there Is a substantial degree of slackness in the economy, in the form of excess productive capacity and idle manpower, budget deficits can provide an important stimulus.
We have had deficit after deficit since this government took office, and we are still waiting for the important stimulus to which the Minister of Finance referred. The minister then went on to stater
By means of such a deficit the government, through its expenditures, places in the hands of the public substantially more purchasing power than it withdraws through taxation. If appropriately planned and timed, a substantial deficit can encourage higher levels of output, employment income and savings, without incurring risks of inflation.
I repeat, this is what this government has been doing since it took office in 1957, and it has failed to create that stimulus which should have benefited the economy of this country. In view of the highest series of deficits in Canadian history, such as the $609 million in 1959 and the $413 million in 1960, has this government succeeded in obtaining the results which it claims it now can achieve with the present forecast deficit of $650 million? If it could accomplish nothing but unemployment in the last three or four years, how can we expect a deficit of $650 million this year to revive the Canadian economy?
I want to repeat what I have said before in the house; that the present government, with its Minister of Finance, is shirking its responsibility. In the first two years of the present government the previous administration was blamed for the state of affairs in the country. When at last they found that their "what would you do" questions were not being taken seriously any more by the general public, they had to put the blame on someone else. We had such statements as we have heard on many occasions from the Minister of Finance and other ministers of the government to the effect that the rate of economic expansion in Europe had shown some hesitation and was having an effect on our country; that conditions in the United States were responsible for the slow-down in Canada.

speechtext:
Let us see what the Minister of Finance had to say about this very same problem just a little over a year ago, on March 31, 1960. I quote the minister's own words as recorded on page 2673 of Hansard:
I have seen some references to a demand that the government should deliberately devalue the dollar. This kind of talk might have been appropriate when Canada was on the gold standard, or even when it maintained a fixed exchange rate. We have not been on the gold standard for half a century and we have not had a fixed exchange rate for a decade.
An attempt by the government artificially to lower the external price of the Canadian dollar would involve borrowing or raising by taxes very large sums of money with which to buy up foreign exchange. It might well be that the government could not reduce the inflow of funds sufficiently without imposing direct controls on capital movements and then on the movement of goods. Apart from the economic objections to such policies it would be a very difficult matter to work out effective technical means of control. Even then the controls would not be effective unless the objective were one which commanded the broad public support which is necessary for general compliance. In other words we would be embarking upon a gigantic financial speculation with no assurance of success.
It would be interesting to know the reasons for such a transformation in the minister's attitude toward devaluation of the dollar. It seems to be generally agreed that had the premium been forced down and kept down some years ago it would have helped Canada keep down the rising costs which now menace our economy. We ask the question, are high living costs going to result from the new policy of the government? We already have indications which lead us to believe this will be the case. With such high costs part of our general way of life, we ask ourselves how effective this action to reduce the dollar premium will be. If the government, even with $1.5 billion in successive deficits, has failed to provide an incentive to promote business and stimulate expansion, how does it expect to succeed by the implementation of these policies? Where is this relief from high costs, this relief from high taxes about which the minister was talking when sitting on the opposition side of the house? The Minister of

The Budget-Mr. Sevigny Finance must admit he has failed to introduce a program which will lift the economy out of the doldrums. He is offering too little too late.
The incentive needed for a move forward is not found anywhere in this budget. If the budget has been so well received in financial, business, banking and commercial circles, it is because the experts recognize that in many ways the budget is an attempt to use fiscal and commercial policies for national purposes. A definite effort is being made to arrange the various taxes in a fashion which will be helpful and stimulating to many segments of the economy.

The government has never claimed that it could, by itself, correct all the ills and worries which have afflicted the businessmen of this nation during the last few years. However, the government does accept the view that business climate-making is one of its basic roles. It has become obvious that because of the measures adopted in last year's budget and also in the so-called baby budget of last November, the bottom of the recent slump has been passed and that our nation can look forward to a long period of definite prosperity. The present budget will permit the business indicators in the forthcoming months to mark progress, and there is no doubt that the people of this country will give credit where it is due. That is to the Conservative government, which has given to Canada a budget which will contribute to the expansion of the nation. Even our severest critics will admit that the budget contains a large number of items which will be beneficial to Canada. In answer to the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River who seems to be so engrossed in his newspaper, I will now name only a few.

The positive improvements and the original thinking which is at the basis of this budget indicate the amount of work that went into its preparation. Some will ask how it is that these measures were not adopted previously. The answer lies in simply stating that there is still a great deal to be done, that caution must at all times be exercised in view of the inflexibility of the present situation, and that great thought must be exercised before stepping forward in any manner or form.
There are, we know, some serious problems which confront the Canadian leaders. The question of chronic unemployment is one. The slow moving upsurge of our secondary manufacturing industries, the serious problem of the continuous increase in foreign ownership, and the imbalance in our foreign payments are all problems of deep concern to those interested in the financial and monetary future of Canada. These basic problems exist and are recognized by the government. It will also be recognized by the people that
The Budget-Mr. Sevigny the measures contained in the budget are steps in the right direction and are intended to correct these ills which unfortunately affect this nation.
There has been a great deal of talk concerning the effects of large imports into our country. There is no doubt in my mind that many industries are seriously affected by the determined efforts of our competitors in foreign lands to rival our Canadian products in our own domestic fields and also in other countries where we offer our merchandise. The problems of these affected industries are of deep concern to us, and we are at all times studying all questions which may permit us to help the situation of these affected industries.
However, it is rather obvious that we cannot tolerate the threatened destruction of certain industries by an exaggerated flow of imports. It also must be realized that if we expect to sell our goods in foreign lands, we must also expect to trade with other countries and to give to foreign businessmen a chance to offer their products to the Canadian public. If we build a thick tariff wall around our nation we shall quickly discourage foreign merchants from considering Canada a nation with which they can trade, and we shall isolate ourselves completely from world markets. This, of course, is most undesirable and cannot be contemplated seriously by those who study the economic picture.
The answer to our problem lies instead in an ever increasing flow of exports which will mean increased production by our manufacturers with the resultant additional employment of labour and the inevitable expansion of premises and manufacturing capacity. In order to increase our exports to foreign lands a high pressure and very effective campaign has already been started by the Minister of Trade and Commerce in order to sell Canada, to sell Canadian products, and especially to sell abroad Canadian know-how. This campaign has been started, is progressing and is bringing immediate results.
In order for this campaign to gain steam it was necessary to take a long, hard look at the present price structure of our products in comparison with the prices of similar goods produced in competitive nations. The study made us realize that in many sectors our Canadian products were possibly not overpriced if we looked at the price structure according to domestic patterns, but were certainly offered at prices which were unattractive to foreign buyers. It is just plain common sense to accept the fact that if a buyer considers two products of similar quality he will almost inevitably purchase the article offered at a lower figure; and it is futile to hope that results can be achieved

The Budget-Mr. Sevigny by those who maintain a rigid price structure and remain inflexible in their bargaining tactics.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at one o'clock I was in the process of explaining the nature of the very strong export drive which had started in Canada, promoted by this government, in order to interest more and more foreign buyers in the quality and the worth of products manufactured in our land. I was mentioning the necessity of being competitive in the pricing of our products, and that it was impossible for Canadian manufacturers to hope to secure orders unless they could offer products of equal quality at prices which were close to those of our competition. I was explaining that the only way we could expect a heavier flow of business was by getting more and more orders from people interested in what we could produce and making these people aware of the fact that our prices were competitive.
It is of course extremely important to bring our prices in line with those offered by our foreign competitors. In this particular field government can help, and the government in fact has done just this in the recent moves which will produce the devaluation of our dollar, which is already quite evident, on world markets. In order to give help to those interested in the export field it is logical to reduce the value of our Canadian dollar. It must be remembered that one of the reasons for Canada's enormous expansion in the immediate post-war years was the fact that our dollar was then below the value of the allpowerful United States currency. There is no doubt that a devalued Canadian dollar will give our merchants an additional incentive which they need to offer Canadian products at competitive prices.
This will mean more sales, more revenue for our manufacturers; and there is no doubt that this additional revenue will be used to expand industries and production facilities. There is also no doubt that since research will be tax free, according to the measures introduced in this budget, a vast program will be undertaken by both our larger and our average industries to improve existing facilities and also in order to find new products which can be produced in Canada and sold in our domestic and foreign markets. This will mean more production and more jobs for our people.


The government is doing its share in this respect, but it must be realized by all Canadian people that government cannot do it all alone. If business is to increase, prosperity will ensue mostly through the combined efforts of all those interested in Canadian trade and Canadian industry. It must be realized that it is a fallacy to expect that this can all be done by the government alone. Charity well ordained begins at home, and those interested in their own welfare must themselves make the individual effort necessary for the prosperity of their business.
There are two things that should be done by private enterprise people in order to increase the amount of business that can be done here in Canada. First of all industry must take a close and very hard look at its price structure and accept the fact that although higher prices may in some cases mean higher revenues, they will also mean a smaller flow of trade. Industry today must try to make its profit more through a large volume of business than through high profits on the individual items.
Industry must also accept the necessity to co-operate with the labour force of Canada. It may be that additional people could be employed if more people worked fewer hours in various factories. Industry must continually be ready to discuss its problems with the labour leaders in a spirit of friendship and co-operation. On the other hand, labour must realize that incessant demands for higher wages or increased benefits can quite easily paralyse the well-ordained plans of industry. Labour must realize that threats which too often result in disastrous strikes are not the answer to the welfare of the individual worker or to the expansion of individual industries. Labour must try to adjust its requests to the capabilities of the employers and only thus, through co-operation between labour and industry, will we achieve the results we seek.
The budget indicates that the resources of the industrial development bank will be increased from the present $160 million to about $400 million. This is a step in the right direction, since it means that a large number of Canadian firms will be permitted to avail themselves of the facilities offered by the industrial development bank. There is no doubt that this is preferable for those who wish to expand to borrow from Canadian sources and pay interest in Canada rather than go to the United States and elsewhere to secure the capital sums required for expansion. The main aim of this extension of the services of the industrial development bank is to help Canadians retain ownership of their companies instead of having to look abroad for new

capital and new investments. This will certainly help all firms which have problems arising from financial consolidations and changes in ownership.
There is no doubt that this question of financing or refinancing private enterprise has presented a very serious problem to the industrialists and manufacturers of this nation. Too many of our people have had to go south of the border or to European countries to try to secure the necessary funds to finance the expansion of their existing business or to build and open up new businesses. Yet there is, here in Canada, a vast source of money, and by affording to our people the chance to borrow this money from the industrial development bank and pay the interest which is normal on such loans we shall make it possible for this money to remain in Canada and work for the better interests of Canadians, thus in the long run enriching the citizens of this country.
There is too little time at my disposal to emphasize the definite gains which will be derived from the new budget by those interested in the automobile industry, the textile industry, the electronics industry and so many other fields of Canadian endeavour. But a study of the budget will permit the realization that this budget has been prepared by men who understand that the expansion of Canada is closely related to the prosperity of our Canadian businessmen. All will benefit from the dynamic measures contained in this expansionist budget, and within a very short time the useful effects of the minister's strategy will be felt in all sectors of our economy. They will be of benefit to Canadian industry, to Canadian business and, in particular, to the labour force and Canadian farm industries.

Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention at this stage of the budget debate to be repetitive in any way in respect to the remarks I made when we were discussing the subamendment. However, because of the limitation of time it was not possible for me at that time to comment in respect to one or two aspects of the presentation made by the Minister of Finance in relation to which I desire to speak this afternoon. I personally feel it rather imperative to answer some of the statements which have been made by the cabinet ministers and backbenchers of the Tory party who have spoken in regard to this matter.
In particular I should like to make some comment regarding the speech we have just heard delivered by the Associate Minister of National Defence. I noted that in the last words of his English presentation he made comments in respect to what he called the Fleming strategy. I suggest it would have been far more appropriate for him to refer to it as the Fleming tragedy. If we try to assimilate the speeches of the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Public Works and the Associate Minister of National Defence, we can only arrive at one conclusion; it is conclusively apparent that the Tory government since it took office some four years ago has been slipping and drifting along with no more knowledge of its destination than a blind man on a raft floating somewhere between the coast of British Columbia and the coast of Hawaii.
It is not very often that I become incensed in this house, but the Associate Minister of National Defence made one remark which, if he had said nothing else, should certainly have brought me to my feet. I refer to that despicable statement he made almost at the beginning of his presentation to the effect that both parties in opposition were doing a disservice to Canada and bringing disgrace upon it because they had the temerity and the daring at this session of parliament to rise not once but many times regarding the serious problem of unemployment. I say that is a despicable statement. He may expect Mr. Coyne to shut up and say nothing, but he need not expect those individuals who realize their responsibilities as members of parliament to do the same.
[Mr. Sevigny.l

I have the honour to represent, as I have represented for a great many years, a constituency in Vancouver which is strictly a working class residential area. After representing it as an M.L.A. and M.P. for 28 years I feel I know my responsibilities to the residents, and one of those responsibilities has regard to employment. If they are unemployed I maintain it is my duty to seek an answer to the situation. According to the Associate Minister of National Defence, to do so is to do a disservice as a member of this house to the people of this country.
I should like to draw to his attention and to the attention of all hon. members of this house the situation which exists in my home city. According to the records I find that from March 1, 1960 until March 31, 1961, a period of 12 months, the unemployment insurance office in the city of Vancouver paid out more than $25 million in unemployment insurance benefits. Why has that office had to do that? I suggest the answer lies in the fact that during that 12-month period there were 134,000 applications for unemployment insurance benefits. Let us not forget that although there may have been 134,000 applications and $25 million paid out in unemployment insurance benefits during that 12-month period, that is not the grand total of unemployment, because many thousands of individuals were not entitled during that period to unemployment insurance benefits.
What do the figures show in relation to the Vancouver unemployment insurance office during that time? Those figures show that in January of this year there were 40,651 individuals drawing unemployment insurance benefits from that one office in Vancouver at a cost of over $3J million. Because this government always likes to refer to the lesser figure, let us consider the best month of that 12-month period, which was July. In July, 20,945 individuals were drawing unemployment insurance benefits from that one Vancouver office at a cost of over $1 million. Taking that 12-month period from March 31, 1960 to March 31, 1961 we find that the average number of unemployed individuals was 5,000 more than during the same period a year before.
The Associate Minister of National Defence has the unmitigated gall to say that because we are representing the people in our constituencies in respect to this matter of unemployment in an attempt to do whatever is possible, we are doing a disservice to this country. Let me suggest that it is not a disgrace to be a responsible member of parliament and to question the government's policy in regard to this situation, but that it is a disgrace on the part of the government,

because it has done nothing about it and has not found a solution to the problem.
I suggest the Associate Minister of National Defence should study basic economics before rising in this house, if he has a desire to intelligently discuss a finance budget. What did he say in this regard? He said, and I quote his words: "Canadians will have to work harder to overcome our disgraceful name overseas."
I think Canadians are prepared to work harder, Mr. Speaker, but we have between 30,000 and 40,000 in the Vancouver area who would love to have the opportunity to work at all, let alone work harder. Produce your policies to produce the jobs. The Associate Minister of National Defence said that really hard work went into the budget. I suppose that is true, but it is too bad that the hard work has not produced more than what we have seen so far.
But even with all that the associate minister said in favour of the budget, what did he also say? I wrote it down as he said it. He said that one of the biggest problems still facing the government is the problem of chronic unemployment. Yes, the minister said that chronic unemployment is still with us, in the same way that R. B. Bennett used to talk about prosperity being just around the corner. The budget does not solve the problem.
The minister also said that we had to be careful about tariffs because tariff walls will isolate us from foreign markets. I agree with him. But what I cannot understand is that a so-called responsible minister should get up, put forward a bunch of rotten window dressing and tell us that increased tariffs will be dangerous and will isolate us, while at the same time completely ignoring the fact that a devalued dollar is the same thing as a tariff increase. A devaluated dollar is a tariff increase because we have to pay for imports in Canadian dollars. Other countries have to export to Canada in order to obtain Canadian dollars, and if we have to pay for those goods with devaluated dollars then for every 1 per cent our dollar goes down in value it is the same as a tariff rise by a similar amount. So why should we have this type of foolishness from one who is supposed to be a responsible minister of the crown?
Why does the government completely ignore the basic facts of economics? I can still hear the eloquence and vehemence of the associate minister when he said that a flow of exports is our goal. We will all agree that a flow of exports should be our goal. We will all agree that everything has to be done to increase our exports. But there the minister stops. We are not going to export for nothing. We have to
The Budget-Mr. Winch be paid for our exports in Canadian dollars, and how do these countries get Canadian dollars unless we import?
The Minister of Finance, the Minister of Public Works, the Associate Minister of National Defence, every backbencher completely ignores that side of the balance sheet. Before we are finished with this budget I think it is going to be very interesting so far as the other side of the balance sheet is concerned if we can get an explanation of Conservative economics that will give some indication that the budget is not simply window dressing, not just wishful thinking; that the government, as I said, is not just drifting like a blind man on a raft between British Columbia and Hawaii, that they have thought things through.
There, of course, is where I challenge them. They have not thought things through. They do not know how to think things through. They are just hoping that something will turn up to rescue them from the fiasco brought about by their own complete and absolute ineptitude. If they carry on as they have for the last four years there is only one rescue, war; and God forbid that that should happen, because it would be suicide for the world. I say, sir, that I just want to take some of the statements made by the cabinet ministers who have already spoken.
However, I do not want only to be critical. Let me offer something they have not thought of that may help a bit. The Minister of Finance has brought in a deficit budget. Without doubt there are times when a deficit budget is in the interests of the country to deal with an immediately serious situation. But I think the Minister of Finance in his presentation has been absolutely unfair in bringing forward a deficit budget without national planning. Let it be remembered that the deficit budget of $650 million-and I do not agree with that figure because with the borrowing they are going to have to do it will be over $1 billion-is tied in with the three previous deficit budgets, and the presentation of a further deficit budget is only an immediate solution to get the government off the hook. What they are doing about national planning is saying to our children and our children's children, "You will pay for the incompetence of this government". The deficit has to be repaid, and it has to be repaid with interest. If we know this government, the deficit is not only going to have to be repaid with interest but the interest is going to have to be paid by further borrowings involving more interest. In other words, it is our children and our children's children who are being asked to pay to get this incompetent government off the hook on which it finds

I say, sir, this is not fair. I imagine our children will have enough problems without us passing on our problems to them. That is what will happen unless, of course, we have a change to a good government.
As I have said, I recognize that the immediate occasion may call for a deficit budget, but at the same time I believe there should be planning along with it. The associate minister said that a lot of work had gone into the budget, but I say that the work was only half done. I suggest that along with a $650 million deficit budget there should have been a policy statement involving government control of investment capital so the government could at least have some direction as to the type of productive work that would be initiated by that investment. I say there should have been a policy of control of excess depreciation reserves. Let us not fool ourselves. Corporation after corporation in Canada is cheating its stockholders, cheating the corporation and cheating the income tax department because of the way it manipulates its depreciation reserves. There should have been some provision in that regard as an offset to the deficit.
This afternoon the Associate Minister of National Defence said so piously that charity begins at home. That being so, why was there not some policy statement and planning with regard to government control of excess profits so as to do what the minister said we should do, and see that the profit-hungry corporations of this country have a decent sense of responsibility? Members may not want to admit it, but these corporations do not have a decent sense of responsibility so far as profits are concerned. They want more and more and more, and the only time they will ever behave is when they are brought under control. It was necessary to control excess profits in time of war, and I say it is still necessary in the critical period through which Canada is passing at the present time.
Yes, the Associate Minister of National Defence really made quite a remark when he said that industry must limit its profits. I am afraid industry will not do so of its own accord, and that is one reason we must have a national government policy. I have mentioned excess profits and I also mention capital gains. When I think of the many speeches about Texas buccaneers made by hon. members opposite when they sat on this side of the house, I also recall that they have been in office four years and as yet they have not done anything about these buccaneers. What is one of the big reasons why money comes into Canada? It is because the


United States has a 25 per cent capital gains tax. Canada, of all the countries in the world, is the happy hunting ground of the financial, monopoly buccaneers of the world. The minister referred to charity beginning at home, and I think it is time that Canada looked at this question of industry limiting its profits.
I could have found a deficit budget far more acceptable if the government had followed through on national planning. I have just given a few indications of what I mean by national planning. Let us go further. I am following along the lines suggested by the Associate Minister of National Defence. During the latter part of his remarks he said that our prices must be competitive. Of course our prices must be competitive if we are going to succeed in the export market. Why then, when the Minister of Finance announced the establishment of a policy to devaluate the Canadian dollar, did he not introduce policies to enable us to remain competitive in the production field?
Of course in my own province the pulp and paper and lumber industries are going to gain some advantage in export markets as a result of the devalued dollar. However, Mr. Speaker, their production costs are going to go up. Why is this? This result will be produced because none of the major machinery required in the pulp and paper and lumber industries is manufactured in Canada. It has to be imported into Canada from the United States. This imported machinery which they must have to maintain production has to be purchased with the devaluated dollar.
Government policy, therefore, is increasing the costs of production of these industries, in spite of the fact that the minister who spoke before me said we have to maintain a competitive level. If the government had thought things through, at the same time they devalued the dollar to aid our exports they would have changed the tariff level on those things which must be imported to maintain our productive capacity. If this had been done we could maintain our present cost of production and not increase it. Both sides of the question have to be considered. This has never been done by the government. They are not facing up to the issues, the practical issues, the financial issues or the economic issues. They are not wearing gold-hued glasses, they are wearing a blindfold. This is dynamite for Canada, to have a government wearing a blindfold.
What I have said with regard to cost of production is also true with regard to the cost of living. The government must have known, if they gave any thought to it at all-surely they have economic advisers who could tell them-that if you devalue the dollar you have

to pay more for your imports. I want to speak now about one thing, and that is the imports into Canada that we do not and cannot produce.
I have spoken about this in relation to manufacturing, but how about the consumers, the forgotten men and women in this budget? Is there anything in this budget to protect them from the devalued dollar as it affects the necessities of life? Has anything been done about coffee, tea, spices, or about the many other things we have to import because it is impossible to grow them or manufacture them here? A government that was thinking across the board, a government that understood economics, a government that had any interest at all in the consumer, when devaluing the dollar would have given some thought to the regulation of the economy so that as the dollar went down in exchange value the tariff would go down correspondingly on those necessities that must be imported so that the standard of living would be maintained. No, sir, we have nothing of that type. Not only does the government not take care of those things that we have to import, but they have not even protected us in relation to those things we grow and manufacture ourselves. Some of these things are already increasing in price.
What I said about the tea, spices, coffee and cocoa is also true of the imported fruits and vegetables which come on the market prior to our own. An announcement has already been made that prices on the Vancouver market for fruits and vegetables are going up this week. My hon. friend laughs. The increase may be half a cent, one cent or two cents, but this means a lot to old age pensioners, blind pensioners, veteran pensioners, in fact to everybody. When it comes to basic economics all these things have been completely ignored.
Why has something not been done directly to encourage Canadian industry? Sometimes I think they do not want to encourage Canadian industry. Let me give one example. I know of a firm that started manufacturing in Vancouver and which now has a manufacturing plant in Ontario, one which is going to mean a great deal in the future. Approximately two thirds of this manufacturer's product is produced in Vancouver or in Clinton, Ontario. About one third has to be imported from the United States. Although this manufacturer has travelled from Vancouver to Halifax he cannot find a plant that can or will produce what is absolutely essential to his product. He has to bring this element in from the United States. He is faced with excise and customs taxes on those items he is forced to import of 27$ per cent plus 10 per cent. Here is a man who is trying to develop a business in Canada and get things
The Budget-Mr. G. Campbell going, yet he is faced with customs and excise taxes of 27$ per cent plus 10 per cent on those elements he cannot obtain in Canada.
I say, sir, it is quite obvious that this budget has not been thought through, that this budget is related to only one side of the question and not to both sides of the question. It is a deficit budget, but its implications have not been considered. I do not think that is right. We hope, Mr. Speaker, that part of it which is good will really work, but we are rather afraid, because the whole budget has not been thought through, the repercussions can be serious. The rosy picture painted by the Minister of Finance and others may not be realized because they refuse to see both sides of the picture.
I want to conclude by saying, and all the supporting speeches made on the budget thus far only indicate, that it has been half thought out and that it is half baked. However, there is still time this session to rectify the omissions, and that is the most important thing. I appeal to the government and to the Minister of Finance. The well-being and the welfare of the people of Canada demand that before this parliament closes, prorogues or is dissolved, the government and the Minister of Finance in particular get busy and overcome their four years of irresponsibility and indecision and give some indication at least that they know something about government planning and administration.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, last week on the public works estimates the hon. member for Laurier neglected the affairs of Laurier and took up the time of this house by making another incursion into Stormont. He is either an incurable busybody or he suffers from an unquiet conscience.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

No. The hon.
