subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is a very reasonable one.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I shall be glad to answer questions afterwards. The hon. member for Laurier put up a smokescreen around all the damage he had done to his home constituency of Stormont by locating the seaway locks on the United States side and then abandoning this constituency like a sinking ship. Now that the present member and the government of which he is a supporter are attempting to rectify some of this damage by erecting a harbour, he is attempting to jump on the band wagon and claim credit for it. The people of Cornwall and the people of

The Budget-Mr. G. Campbell the St. Lawrence valley know that the time to have built a Canadian seaway was when the seaway was being constructed. No 27-foot channel ending in an 80-foot wall is a substitute for a Canadian seaway. The disastrous decline in tonnage on the Cornwall canal is due not to the competition of air lines, buses or trucks, as the hon. member for Laurier alleged, but is due to the fact that the Cornwall canal is now a stagnant backwater which also ends in a blank wall. The traffic now passes through the United States seaway locks.
If the new industrial complex adjacent to the seaway locks was the result of cheap power in New York state, as the hon. member contends, rather than the United States seaway locks, then why on earth did not the hon. member, who did all the seaway dealings for his government, and his provincial Liberal colleague in Ontario not endeavour to protect the interests of this area? Obviously the time to have extracted concessions from Ontario hydro was when the joint project was being constructed, at this time when the Ontario hydro were looking out for all of Ontario by putting the power from this area on the Ontario grid in the same way the power from Niagara Falls serves the whole of the province of Ontario.
I should also like to ask the hon. member for Laurier how much of the $800 million spent on the seaway that he boasts so much about went to Cornwall people, as he alleged, and how much went to Montreal and Toronto contractors. My precedessor also said that the former municipal administration in Cornwall spent $140,000 to expropriate land at Gray's creek at Cornwall for harbour purposes on the recommendation of the C.N.R. economic survey, which he no doubt ordered himself. The overburdened taxpayers of Cornwall will be very much interested indeed in knowing who is responsible for this large and so far useless expenditure, with all the interest that has accrued thereon.
Last year I informed this House of Commons of the assassination of a city by its favourite son and of its betrayal by the former minister of transport.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No one ever did as much for Cornwall as the hon. member for Laurier.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
This hon. member tried to justify himself again last week on the estimates. He can twist and squirm till the cows come home, but he will not get off the hook. When I was a boy down on the farm, if a trusted dog killed a chicken we tied it around his neck until it rotted. The


hon. member for Laurier today has a chicken tied around his neck called Cornwall seaway city.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is it eviscerated?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is eviscerated. The people of Stormont and the people of Laurier see it every time they look at him. He is a desolate man. By night he is haunted by the ghosts of two stillborn infants called the Canadian seaway locks. By day he is pursued by two illegitimate children born of a United States mother and1 called the Eisenhower and Snell locks. There are persistent rumours in northern New York state that the people of Massena, the village across the river from Cornwall, are going to erect a suitable monument to the father of the Snell and Eisenhower locks. They say that that mausoleum in Cornwall, that consolation prize for Cornwall-I refer to the St. Lawrence seaway headquarters building which he erected as a monument to himself-is not appreciated there. It is located in the wrong country.
I did not intend to go into the matter of the budget, but I cannot allow this opportunity to go by without saying a few words on unemployment insurance and the budget. I firmly believe that this latest budget will do very much to hasten the economic recovery which is evident not only in Canada but in the United States. However, it is quite possible that with the increased automation we have throughout North America and indeed throughout the world we shall still have a large measure of structural unemployment even during periods of economic booms and expansion. If so, I should like to make a few suggestions regarding unemployment insurance and such matters for the consideration of the government.
My first suggestion is this. I believe it is desirable that the age of retirement be lowered to 60 years and that we spend more money on contributory old age pensions and less on unemployment insurance. It is desirable that older men enjoy the evening of their years in comfort and leisure so that men in the prime of life can have the jobs that will provide for their families and enable them to retain their self-respect.
I now proceed to my second suggestion. British Columbia fishermen have been known on occasion to make as much as $8,000 to $10,000 in several months if they get an exceptionally good catch. Loggers sometimes make the same amount during a cutting season of five to six months. Women who happen to be married to prosperous businessmen or professional men often quit work after a few months owing to pregnancies or for other reasons. In each of these three

cases, and no doubt in other similar instances, these people draw unemployment insurance for the remainder of the year. When the breadwinner of a family has a total annual income exceeding a certain ceiling-and that ceiling, of course, can vary with the number of children or other dependents-I believe that he or his spouse should not be eligible for unemployment insurance for the remainder of that year. If the regulations were changed in this respect it would not only reduce government expenditures but would be conducive to thrift, self-reliance and independence in our people.
My third and final suggestion with regard to unemployment is more far-reaching. I believe there should be a fluctuating scale of unemployment insurance payments varying with the degree of unemployment in the country. When unemployment is high the payments could be almost as high as the average person's income over the past three to five years. These high unemployment insurance payments would maintain consumer purchasing power at a high level, thus encouraging production in the country and increasing the number of jobs. When prosperity returns; when unemployment drops and jobs are plentiful, then the unemployment insurance payments could be reduced to a mere subsistence level. When unemployment is high, if some loafers do not want jobs it does not matter very much anyway because there are no jobs available; but when jobs are plentiful the low payments would induce them to go out and find one.
I realize that these suggestions will require very careful study and I think they would be difficult and complicated to administer. But if we can invent atomic bombs, it should not be beyond the wit of man to devise practical means of providing economic security in such a rich country as Canada. These suggestions with regard to unemployment insurance have the great merit, in my opinion, of fitting into our present economic system with a minimum of dislocation and without resorting to a socialistic planned economy.
I cannot resist a few comments on the budget and on the crisis in the Bank of Canada. First let me commend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) for resisting the urgent demand of the governor of the bank that he raise income taxes. Let me commend the minister on the aid his budget has given to the hard pressed textile and automobile industries. Let me further commend the minister on increasing the scope and resources of the industrial development bank. More than one motel in Stormont that I know of will be saved from bankruptcy if they take advantage of these provisions.
The Budget-Mr. G. Campbell
Let me especially commend the minister on reducing the exchange value of our dollar, which is the equivalent of a 5 per cent general increase in tariffs, to protect secondary industry at home and a 5 per cent general reduction in costs to assist our primary industries to sell abroad. Nothing could possibly do more at this time to stimulate our economy than this measure. Mr. Coyne's proposal, for a 10 per cent surcharge on tariffs, may be desirable but, like most of his suggestions, it is academic and entirely impractical because of our international treaty obligations, many of which were incurred by our predecessors.
Let me further commend the minister on his responsibility and restraint under extreme provocation in trying to work out some peaceable basis of co-existence with Mr. Coyne until his term of office expires at the end of this year. The minister did all that was humanly possible to avoid bringing the Bank of Canada into disrepute, but the governor's exhibitionist antics in calling an unprecedented press conference, in releasing his own budget statements and in exposing numerous confidential letters caused this whole unseemly explosion. Let me finally comment the minister on his refusal to bring this matter before a committee of the House of Commons, which would produce the kind of circus that would cause a crisis in confidence in the economy of this country throughout the world.
May I say also to the minister that if I were minister of finance Mr. Coyne would long ago have been fired as he deserved, and he would have been exposed to the ridicule of a parliamentary committee as he requests. That is probably one of the reasons why I am not minister of finance. May I say, further, that he would probably be in jail for misappropriation approaching larceny in using the facilities of the Bank of Canada to promote his private purposes; or if not on that indictment, for a breach of confidence approaching perjury in broadcasting the internal affairs of the bank in defiance of his oath of office.
In this whole unsavoury matter we must not lose sight of the fundamental issue involved. This fundamental issue is very, very simple indeed. It is this: who is running the country? Is it parliament and the people, or the bankers and the bureaucrats? The last time any parliament set up under the British system was challenged to this extent by any one man who was not representing the people was in 1611-and King Charles lost his head. If the Liberals had any conception at all of how our constitution works they would not be defending Mr. Coyne; they would be impeaching him, for he has usurped the functions of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. HOUSE OF COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. G. Campbell Pearson) whose prime duty it is to criticize the government. There Js an old proverb, Mr. Speaker: Whom the gods would destroy they first make mad.
I have here a fantastic letter, a letter such as never before in this country has passed between a public servant and a people's government. It is the latest scandal sheet put out by Mr. Coyne. The instigator of this scurrilous letter could only be the same pathological man whose conduct we witnessed in the House of Commons last night. May I ask the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill)-I see he is not here, but I shall ask him at the earliest opportunity; no doubt my words will be conveyed to him and I would like an answer-whether he also supports Mr. Coyne in his bid to take over the leadership of the Liberal party; or does the hon. member prefer Mr. Charles Templeton, the apostate evangelist and C.B.C. actor? Which is his choice?
It is a pitiful sight, Mr. Speaker, to see gentlemen who were once honourable behaving like carrion, snapping at the dry bones of the leadership of a once great party. Even the younger and the more virile elements in this party, or what is left of it, have such a death wish that they hope to submerge themselves in the arms of the socialists. I need not waste much time on the antics of Mr. Coyne, which are known to all hon. members only too well. He went up and down this country preaching austerity and yet he voted himself, in the most clandestine manner, a pension for life of $25,000 annually after only six years of service.
Let me say further that that very great gentleman for whom I have always had the utmost respect, Rt. Hon. Louis St. Laurent, after 17 years of outstanding service in this house, during each of which he contributed toward his pension, now receives $3,000 per year less about $660 for old age pension. This is a standard of comparison. Mr. Coyne went about preaching; he pleaded with us; he pleaded with the government, with the country and with the ordinary housewife to reduce our imports, and yet he ordered custom-made cars from Kalamazoo, Michigan, for himself and his staff to ride around in. Then he criticized this government in a most political and partisan way, but when he was called before a Senate committee largely made up of his own political sympathizers, what had he to say? He had no cure; he had no panacea; he had not even a constructive suggestion to offer about the economy-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext:
May I say, Mr. Speaker, that there has been more confusion and more controversy among this government and its predecessor and the Bank of Canada in the last six years than there was in the previous 20 years under Mr. Graham Towers, who incidentally was appointed by Mr. R. B. Bennett. Mr. Graham Towers served his country in this position with distinction and competence. There is another basis of comparison.
Leading professors of economics in our Canadian universities, Mr. McLaughlin of the Royal Bank and most of our leading bankers, our union leaders and most responsible people in this country insist and indeed demand that this governor must go. Even the societe generale de Belgique and other leading foreign financial houses in their bulletins distributed to their customers and clients throughout the world insist that confidence in the Canadian economy will be restored only with his passing. Yet we see in this house the members of the official opposition being his most valiant supporters.
May I say in closing that the Minister of Finance has the best possible precedent for his present action. Christ chased the money lenders from the temple when they became too arrogant. The Minister of Finance is, as it were, chasing them from the government in asking for the resignation of Mr. Coyne, who threatens the existence of the government by his arrogance.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Tuesday night, June 20, the whole country which had been waiting for a long time for its health report, heard the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) put forward in a very long and rather confused speech what he intended to do for the 1961-62 fiscal year.
The main theme of his speech, that night, was that he was introducing a budget of economic expansion and that, to this end, he intended to give Canada fiscal, financial and trade policies calculated to create more jobs, stimulate production, in a word, to improve the general state of our national economy.
Since this administration took over the Minister of Finance introduced four budgets and in every one of them, he gave indications of optimism and hope about Canada's economic situation.
In 1958, with a deficit, the Minister of Finance said he had inherited from the Liberals a bad economic and commercial situa-

tion, and especially unemployment, and that it was imperative to make adjustments in the then forthcoming year.
In 1959, with a deficit of $609 million, the minister admitted that there had been a recession, adding that our economy was recovering, and he predicted results and a marked reduction of the number of unemployed.
In 1960, after forecasting a surplus of $12 million and offering optimistic indications about the country's economy and the revenues that would accrue to the government, the minister expressed the idea that it was time we came back to a policy of balanced budgets. Of course the minister's aim was poor, since the forecast of a $12 million surplus was changed in fact to a deficit of $345 million.
With regard to his desire to have a balanced budget, this is what the Minister of Finance said last year, as reported on page 2681 of Hansard:
-and in my budget speech a year ago 1 recommended to this house policies which were designed to bring us back to a position of budgetary balance as soon as the economy had recovered the losses of the recession and was moving firmly forward and upward to new record achievements in production, employment and investment.
The position we have now reached, with its sound prospect of a fully balanced budget, represents the fruits of carefully designed policies carried forward over the past 18 months. This is not something that has just happened. It is the result of considered aims and efforts.
As can be seen, Mr. Speaker, the minister was quite sure of himself, but "the result of considered aims and efforts" was not very good since the whole thing turned into a deficit.
Each time he presents a budget, the Minister of Finance announces that the economy is recovering and that the situation is again flourishing but, when he tables his next budget, he never admits that he was mistaken; he merely says that things are seen under a different light.
In the present budget, the minister tells us that the steps he advocates, such as the free devaluation of the dollar and the reduction of the interest rates, will not create inflation.
However, he does not give any reason to justify that statement. The devaluation of the dollar will mean more money for the tradesman, the businessman and the industrialist, but what about the small wage-earner and the labourer?
When I studied political science, I learned that the devaluation of a country's currency means a premium on exports. There can be no mistake but that our exports will increase, that tradesmen, businessmen will make more
The Budget-Mr. Meunier money, but will those surpluses result in a lower salary for workers and labourers? We do not know. But on the other hand, it is obvious that the price of our imports will climb and without listing them all, I have in mind certain essential commodities such as tea, coffee, sugar, cocoa and other products of which our families are in constant need. Who is going to pay, when the price of those commodities goes up? It will be the low-income people, the wage earners, the labourers, and if those people's incomes do not increase they will be faced with a rise in the cost of living which they will not be able to bear.
On that point, I should like to quote the statement of Mr. Donald MacDonald, secretary-treasurer of the Labour Congress, as reported in La Presse, last June 22.
The federal budget contains no improvement in the field of social security, no true relief for the small taxpayer, nothing which is likely to increase substantially the consumer's purchasing power.
I regret that the minister did not give us his views on that point, and although I could ask him several questions on that matter, I will merely ask him one.
If the government must borrow money to finance its budget deficit, what will happen to the loans that municipalities, provinces or big business will have to raise abroad?
What will be the loss resulting from the exchange rate for the provinces and the municipalities which have already borrowed money abroad?
Has the government provided anything to allow public bodies to borrow more easily to finance their debt or undertake large scale projects in order to reduce unemployment?
The minister told us that his expansionist budget would create more jobs, would stimulate industry and increase production. Those words are delightful to hear, but I would have liked to know from the minister to what extent that expansion will go and how many jobs that new policy will create.
The minister is asking the provinces and the municipalities to raise a large part of their loans in Canada. I do not question the minister's good intention because it is a very desirable objective. But, if the government drains the market to finance its loans, what will be left to the provinces and the municipalities? They will be forced to go on foreign markets and to repay their matured loans with devaluated dollars. It means that they will find themselves paying millions of dollars that they did not expect to pay.
How will all that balance? We know nothing about that, because the minister provided no

The Budget-Mr. Meunier explanation. It would have been interesting to have his views on that point, in which case he would have not only enlightened the people on the matter but also made the borrowers aware of the effects of this measure.
I mentioned a few minutes ago that the Minister of Finance had stated that all those policies he was advocating would create jobs, but that he did not give us any idea of the number of jobs which would result for the Canadian people.
There constantly exist in Canada, Mr. Speaker, certain vague conditions which cannot escape being noticed by everyone, a chronic and gnawing disease to which the government does not seem to pay too much attention: unemployment.
I appreciate that since the beginning of the present session, the government has enacted legislation conceived to relieve unemployment. I am aware of such things as the productivity council, assistance to technical and vocational schools, financial assistance to small enterprise, double depreciation and amendments to the National Housing Act. It is true, Mr. Speaker, that all those measures are going to help create jobs and reduce unemployment.
But I do not agree that housing is going to remedy unemployment, because it has been found that Montreal, the metropolis of Canada, is also the city with the most houses to let. When the government got elected in 1957, it invested heavily in building. On the other hand, I recall that in 1957, the Hon.
C.	D. Howe, addressing the lumber dealers association, said that house building had to keep a steady pace because activity in the building trade is a sign of prosperity.
What happened is that we invested heavily in building and as a result, the price of the building lots went up. Houses are nowadays selling at prohibitive prices. And with the land selling at prohibitive prices, some builders have gone out of business.
I heard on television that in the city of Montreal, building had increased 4.6 per cent last year. That is no stimulus and no way of creating many jobs.
It is in the field of one-family units that the situation is most disastrous. A house is sold to a buyer who is asked a ridiculously low down payment. Enthused, he wants to have his own home. He goes visiting housing developments. He is told that he will have to pay only so much a month. But what happens is that when the municipality starts putting in sewers, waterworks and other services, the assessments increase and the

amount the buyer expected to pay annually is changed. In addition, those who buy one-family houses in suburban Montreal have to buy a car for transportation, and after two or three years, which is not so surprising, the buyer cannot fulfil his obligations any more and has only one alternative, to give the house back to C.M.H.C.
I do not think that housing creates so many jobs and that it is the solution to the unemployment problem. Proof of that is in the still sizeable number of our unemployed.
I have here an article of La Presse of June 24 last, written following an interview with Mr. Charles Renaud, director of the department of social welfare of the city of Montreal. I quote:
2,740 needy unemployed in Montreal.
And the article goes on:
In the month of May, 5.8 per cent of the 46,500 unemployed in Montreal were ini dire need.
The 2,740 unemployed in question were no longer entitled to unemployment insurance benefits. Their unemployment insurance benefits were exhausted, and they had to rely on the social welfare service of the municipality for their subsistence. Naturally, they came under unemployment assistance and had to satisfy themselves with what they were given for their subsistence. Those people have no jobs at all. When are they going to work? God knows.
Before concluding my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I should like to reply to certain statements made by the Associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Sevigny). After having praised the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming), he told us that his budget would be beneficial to Canadians. He made a digression to say that the people of Quebec who are interested in Canada's economic life will find something beneficial in this budget. I do not agree with the Associate Minister of National Defence on that point and I suggest to him that, quite to the contrary, all Quebeckers are interested in Canada's economic life, as are all other Canadians.
He told us of the climate of confidence that prevails in the relations between the government and the businessmen in our community. Of course since June 22, 1960, there is a climate of confidence in the province of Quebec between the government and the Quebec businessmen.
But the Associate Minister of National Defence wanted to go back 15 years and

promote again the idea of erecting a monument to Mr. Duplessis, a matter of which we do not hear any more in Quebec. He wanted to tell us that Mr. Duplessis always sought, during the 15 years of his administration in the province of Quebec, to draw all the advantages he could out of his relations with Ottawa, to the benefit of the people of Quebec.
Well, I must tell the Associate Minister of National Defence that he is badly mistaken. For 15 years, Mr. Duplessis, for political expediency purposes, always criticized the Ottawa government, always tried to debase the authority of the government in Ottawa and to have the population of Quebec believe that Ottawa was not our country's capital, out that of a foreign country.
Now, if Mr. Duplessis has always taken advantage of federal legislation, as the Associate Minister of National Defence claims, I will say for his information that, because of Mr. Duplessis' stubbornness the province of Quebec lost in 15 years close to $1 billion, and here is how. In never wanting to participate in joint plans for forest protection; in never wanting to participate in joint plans for the construction of the trans-Canada highway; in refusing to co-operate in fiscal matters from 1944 to 1956; in refusing to accept grants for vocational schools.
Mr. Duplessis, logical in his autonomy, refused at that time to accept the federal government's money for vocational schools. During all the time Mr. Duplessis was at the head of the province of Quebec, I repeat for the Associate Minister of National Defence, the province lost $1 billion. If Quebec had that money today, perhaps there would not be so much unemployment in the province, and Quebeckers might be happier.
The Associate Minister of National Defence said, on two different occasions, that the opposition was singing dirges of gloom and doom and was voicing nothing but destructive criticism. I would say to the Associate Minister of National Defence that if he was unable to be in the house, he should at least have read the official report of debates to be better informed.
Last year, the house discussed the estimates of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) for 12 days. At that time the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) and the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) submitted to the Minister of Labour their proposals for an over-all plan to reduce unemployment.
The Budget-Mr. Meunier The hon. member for Laurier mentioned then that in 1945, when this country was in a transition period from war to peace, and our soldiers were coming back from overseas, an economic emergency had to be faced, and added that the Hon. C. D. Howe, then the minister of reconstruction, had tabled a white book in which he planned for the reconstruction of the country by means of an eight point over-all program to help our economy, which was to be carried out over a period of 15 years.
Now, again last year, as I was saying a few moments ago, hon. members for Laurier and Essex East submitted some constructive suggestions, and the government did not follow up any of those suggestions which formed an over-all plan to help remedy unemployment; nothing was done. Therefore, it ill becomes the Associate Minister of National Defence to say today that the opposition not only is singing dirges of doom and gloom, but fails to make any constructive criticism.
Mr. Speaker, the budget submitted by the Minister of Finance is a mess of high-sounding words. The Associate Minister of National Defence asked us to put our trust in this budget. He sees in it the corner stone of a remarkable development and maintains that thanks to the measures that are provided in it we will at least have a climate favourable to employment. Mr. Speaker, I want to stress that we must always take the budget of the Minister of Finance with a grain of salt. It is the fourth one which he has submitted, and, each year, he describes the situation as encouraging, saying that it is far from alarming, and the following year, as conditions have not improved, he still finds comforting words for describing it. But nothing happens.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I submit that we are right in not trusting the Minister of Finance, because this fourth budget submitted to us proves worse than the previous ones.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to join with other members of the house in congratulating the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) on his budget which will be welcomed by Canada, a budget designed to increase employment and expand the economy. The pleasing aspect of the budget is the fact that there is no increase in taxes, a fact that points up the faith, and justified faith, that the government has in the Canadian people and the Canadian economy.
The retention of the tariff on turkeys and the new five to ten cents per pound tariff on dressed chickens will be of great aid to our farmers. Tariff adjustments will be welcomed by the textile industry, although apparently the minister did not go far enough for the hon. member for Drummond-Artha-baska (Mr. Boulanger). He advocates the imposition of dumping duties on textiles. The hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) would like to impose higher tariffs on automobiles and parts entering Canada. Hon. members of the Liberal party have been advocating the adoption of the proposals of the governor of the Bank of Canada, increased taxes, increased tariffs and trade restrictions. How do they reconcile their present attitude with previous public statements? The views on tariffs of the member for Essex East, the spokesman for the party, seem to vary daily. People are rapidly reaching the conclusion that this is due to a complete lack of Liberal policy, cynical application of the divide and rule theory and political expediency of the moment.
The position of the third party was expressed by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier). I assume he was speaking for his party when he stated in the house that he did not believe in tariffs. He preferred quotas and currency restrictions, the most vicious form of protectionism ever designed. The present government, in contrast with the opposition groups, is fully aware that Canadian prosperity depends on world trade, that high tariffs and restrictions have no place in our economy. The government policy is one of moderation designed to ensure a fair balance between all segments of the economy. The reduction of the sales tax on various items is welcome. The automobile industry will benefit and the consumer will benefit.

The municipalities have been requesting direct aid from the federal government. I do not know whether this is possible under our system of government, but the addition of further items to the long list of sales tax exempt materials required by municipalities, payment of 50 per cent of the labour costs on municipal projects under the winter works program, credit for the inception and extension of which must be given to this government, increased hospital construction grants and the new grants for equipping and building technical schools have been of great assistance to the municipalities and the taxpayers.
All branches of the pharmaceutical profession have recently been receiving a great deal of publicity with respect to the high cost of pharmaceuticals and pharmaceutical preparations. The critics were not well enough nor fully enough informed to justify their sweeping generalizations. It is for this reason that the profession welcomes the public inquiry to be conducted under the Combines Investigation Act. If the investigation should show that any segment of the profession is conspiring to maintain prices at an unwarranted level, I am sure the profession itself will take steps to remedy the situation.
The cost of medicine to the sick could be reduced by the removal of the sales tax on those ingredients used in medicinal preparations. I confess to extreme disappointment that this step was not taken in the present budget. I urge the Minister of Finance to give this suggestion careful consideration. If it would not be practical to remove the sales tax on the whole range of medicinal products, consideration might be given to removing the tax on those drugs and preparations contained in the schedules of the Food and Drugs Act and the provincial pharmacy acts, that is, for drugs and preparations that can be supplied to a customer only on the signed authorization of a doctor.
The pharmaceutical profession in all its phases is vitally concerned with the physical welfare of Canadians. There was deep disappointment throughout the profession when it was not given representation on the royal commission on health. It is felt by this group so closely associated with the health problems of Canadians that the inclusion of one of their members on the royal commission would have made a substantial contribution to the findings of the commission. I would ask the government to consider including a member of the pharmaceutical profession on the commission.
I listened with great interest to the hon. member for Niagara Falls (Miss LaMarsh). Perhaps my interest was due to the personal charm of the member and the ease of

delivery. Certainly I could not maintain my interest in the hon. member's speech when reading Hansard. The whole speech was particularly sterile. The hon. member intoned with pathos: We have drought in the west which is deepening; we have insects in the west, and so on. These were words that would lead her listeners to think that she really believed that drought, grasshoppers and cutworms were the visitation of a higher power to punish the prairie people for daring to vote anything but Liberal. Bathos!
The members from the prairie provinces know that there is drought in certain areas; grasshoppers, cutworms and a late June frost hit others. The obvious relish with which the Liberal speakers catalogue these disasters leaves a sour taste in our mouths. We are too familiar with the hardship and frustration suffered by our farmers in affected areas. The members of this government are more concerned with devising ways to relieve the hardships caused by the ravages of nature. The Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) announced this morning that emergency measures are now in effect to meet the situation. The Liberal leader could only suggest that the house go into committee of supply to debate crop conditions. That is all they have ever done for the western farmer-talk.
The hon. member for Niagara Falls went on to say: "Many members of this house were children as I was", referring to the 1930-39 period. In discussing the events of the period, the hon. member apparently suffered a lapse of memory. Since I am slightly more mature, my recollection of the period will not be so childish. I believe, if my memory is correct, that a Liberal government came into power in 1935. That year was not a profitable year on the prairies; we had drought, grasshoppers, Russian thistle and extremely low prices. The following year, 1936, saw a continuation of these conditions. The year 1937 saw what was, probably, the most complete crop failure in the history of the prairies. The years 1938 and 1939 showed little, if any, improvement. I would not insinuate that the prime minister of that day was responsible for the vicissitudes of nature, but what were the members of that Liberal government doing, other than sitting on the benches wringing their hands with the attitude, the Almighty will look after us and we will collect taxes where we can? I repeat, what were the Liberal government doing in the face of business stagnation, rampant poverty and unemployment? They did nothing, yes, absolutely nothing, to their everlasting discredit and shame.
The year 1939 marked the outbreak of the war. Checking back on the statistics for that year provides interesting reading. In spite of
The Budget-Mr. Clancy the large number of Canadians who hastened to enlist, unemployment was very high, business was unsettled. The war years, ah yes, that was the period. Controls were slapped on the economy. It was a wonderful world for those forming the government. There were no decisions to make because world events had taken that need out of their hands. There was nothing to do but administer. Those superbureaucrats proceeded to foster and promote the growth of the biggest bureaucracy in the history of the nation.
Canadian farm income, in spite of worldwide shortages, showed only moderate gains in the post-war years. Obviously, there had been no effort to put the economy on a peacetime footing. The Korean war gave a boost to the economy. Farm income rose rapidly until 1951, and levelled off in 1952. The nations of the world were stockpiling for an emergency. From 1952 to 1954, farm income fell rapidly to the 1946 level; a slight increase in 1955 and 1956 was followed by a sharp decline until June 1957. After eleven years, two wars and the death of half a million Canadians, the country was back where it started. Farm income was reduced to nearly the 1946 level, with a rising cost of living, unsettled business conditions and rising unemployment. Indeed, this is a remarkable record.
When the present government took over, steps were taken to strengthen and improve the economic position of our farmers. The improvement has been steady, but perhaps not as rapid as hoped because we were too optimistic in expecting to clean up, in 22 months, the mess left on our doorstep by 22 years of mismanagement and incompetence of a Liberal government.
This government has replaced indifference with positive legislation and action. In the first three years under this government, Canadian agriculture producers have received $499 million from the federal government, an increase of 111 per cent, compared with the last three year period under the previous administration. The 1959-60 payment of $190.9 million was 112 per cent more than the largest payment made in any year by a Liberal administration.
This government paid 50 per cent of the unharvested grain assistance; 50 per cent of the cost of moving equipment and fodder into, and livestock out of, drought areas; instituted cash advances on grain; introduced and put into effect the Farm Credit Act, increasing the maximum amount and repayment period of loans; widened the scope of farm credit and pegged the interest rate for these loans at 5 per cent; introduced Canada's first Crop Insurance Act, under which the government will pay 50 per cent of the

The Budget

Mr. Clancy administration, 20 per cent of the premium and will loan provinces 75 per cent of the amounts required to meet indemnity requirements; paid out $82.6 million in acreage payments; increased the compensation for cattle slaughtered in the control of tuberculosis and brucellosis; undertook to pay 75 per cent of the cost of the South Saskatchewan dam.
The water level of the Saskatchewan and Qu'Appelle valleys will be controlled so that use may be made of waters which were for many years wasted. This government also raised the maximum amount of farm improvement loans from $5,000 to $7,500 and eliminated the double security clause on loans over $2,000; 15 per cent more farmers now benefit under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act as a result of the Conservative government's amendments. The Agricultural Rehabilitation and Development Act has been passed. The Conservative government's program under this act will operate in three ways to rehabilitate and develop Canadian agriculture. It will provide for the development of alternative uses for marginal agricultural land; assist local groups in developing new income opportunities; provide projects for soil and water conservation. So that western grain producers will not have to pay storage charges on wheat stocks in excess of the normal carryover, the Conservative government paid storage charges amounting to $39.8 million in 1958, $43.6 million in 1959 and $51.7 million in 1960. Wheat exports have risen substantially due to an aggressive selling campaign and Canada's increased contributions of wheat and flour to the Colombo plan.
These are a few and by no means all the steps taken to help Canadian agriculture. The Agricultural Stabilization Act is a new approach to the problem of stabilizing farm prices. The act is basically sound. Minor adjustments have been necessary. Snags were bound to develop that only experience in the application of the act could reveal. There are adjustments that are still necessary. I speak now of the operation of the act with respect to hogs and eggs. Under the present regulations the prairie farmers are not receiving full benefit of the act with respect to hogs and eggs. I am not satisfied that the present regulations are fair to the farmers in my area. The farmers are not satisfied.
Let us look at the hog situation. The prescribed price is $23.65 per hundredweight Toronto, on a quota of 100 hogs per producer. A deficiency payment is made when the national weighted average price is below $23.65. The present transportation differential


between Regina and Toronto cannot be justified and the differential should be narrowed.
It is possible to have a situation develop where there is no deficiency payment by using the national weighted average, and yet, the prairie producer will have received a price for his hogs below the prescribed price.
The situation with respect to eggs is more extreme. The prescribed price is 33 cents per dozen Toronto-Montreal for Grade A-XL and Grade A-L with a quota of 1,000 dozen per producer per quarter. The transportation differential between Regina and Toronto is not warranted. The use of the national weighted average price is not fair to the producers in Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba. Let us take an example. The cumulative national weighted average price to producers for Grade A-XL and A-L was 31 cents per dozen on June 10 this year. If there were to be a deficiency payment for this period, it would be two cents per dozen. The weighted average price per dozen during this period for the three prairie provinces is 23.9 cents; British Columbia, 33.2 cents; central Canada,
33.05	cents; the maritimes, 33.4 cents, and Newfoundland, 47.9 cents. The prairie producer would receive 25.9 cents as a final payment, the other areas would receive from
35.05	to 49.9 cents per dozen. The inequality between the prairie region and the other areas in Canada is obvious.
I urge the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hamilton) to give serious and immediate consideration to equalizing with the rest of Canada the returns received by producers in the prairie provinces. I would suggest that deficiency payments on eggs be made quarterly. The producer can receive a deficiency payment only on a maximum of 1,000 dozen per quarter. In other words, if he markets 800 dozen in the first quarter, 700 dozen in the second quarter, 3,000 dozen in the third quarter and 3,000 dozen in the fourth quarter, he can receive a deficiency payment on only 3,500 dozen, although he exceeded the 4,000 dozen maximum for the year.
I suggest that the calculation for deficiency payments should be based on a regional weighted average price for British Columbia, the three prairie provinces, central Canada, the maritimes and Newfoundland. This method would be fair to producers across Canada and would place the prairie farmer on a more nearly equal footing. The stabilization board and the advisory committee recommend that the present system be continued for the balance of the year. I do not agree. Mr. Speaker, I repeat that I believe this is a matter of urgency which should receive immediate and careful consideration by the Minister of Agriculture and the government.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on June 20 last, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) introduced his budget for the fiscal year 1961-62. The people have proved that they had been anxiously awaiting the budget speech, because on that occasion, the galleries of the house were filled to capacity, and most hon. members were in their places.
I also noted a striking difference between the situation prevailing in this house in 1957, and the situation on June 20 last. In 1957, the present Minister of Finance brought down his first budget, and on that occasion, every hon. member on the government side including the Minister of Finance had a nice smile and wore a blue tinted white carnation in his lapel. This year, no one wore a blue tinted white carnation, no one had a flower in his lapel, and at the end of the minister's speech, you could see on the faces of Conservative members an expression of disappointment and discontent. Needless to say, cabinet members did not display the broad smile they had in 1957.
The budget speech of last week was the longest in all the history of Canada, but that is not its main feature. The Minister of Finance has forecast the highest deficit ever recorded by a peacetime government. But this deficit budget does not surprise the Canadian people, because ever since the Conservative government took office, we have only had deficit budgets. In 1958, Canada had a deficit of $38,500,000; the deficit reached $609,500,000, in 1959, $413 million in 1960, and $300 million in 1961. For the year 1962, the minister tells us that the deficit will range from $650 to $700 million, which makes up a total deficit of more than $2 billion for the four years in office of the present government.
Mr. Speaker, there is in my province and in the country a common saying to the effect that when the Conservatives are in office, we have deficits, tax increases, unemployment, tight money, high interest rates, numerous bankruptcies, a higher cost of living, in short, drudgery and hardship for a great many Canadian citizens.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is often said that history repeats itself. We are witnessing today a recurrence of history in this country. Many of us lived through the years 1930 to 1935 under a Conservative administration. And what is the difference between the situation which existed in this country between 1930 and 1935 and that existing today?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is even worse.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I agree that there is a difference, and it is because from 1935 to 1957 the country was run by a Liberal administration which prepared everything and provided for a Conservative administration.
When the Liberals were in power, they took action to remedy unemployment. In 1941, they put in the statute books the Unemployment Insurance Act and, from 1941 to 1957, the unemployment insurance fund reached over $900 million. Since the Conservatives took over, in 1957, the fund has dropped from $900 million to less than $100 million.
Not only did the Liberal party give the country the Unemployment Insurance Act, but they adopted a series of social security measures. There was the Family Allowances Act, a piece of legislation which was not quite welcomed by certain Conservatives when it was introduced in this house. Among all the electoral promises of the Conservative party, I have never seen any to the effect that the Conservative government would increase family allowances.
The Liberal party also provided for pensions for the aged, the disabled and the blind persons.
Mr. Speaker, if the people of Canada did not have today all those social security measures, I am sure that the situation, on account of the high cost of living, would be worse than between 1930 and 1935.
True enough, the budget announces certain tax reductions, of which the most important is the abolition of the excise tax on passenger cars. I am satisfied with that decrease, but I should like or rather I would have liked it better had the minister thought also of our

The Budget-Mr. Leduc farmers, settlers, workers who have to buy a small half-ton truck and forgo the passenger car. It seems to me that the minister should also have abolished the excise tax on half-ton trucks.
The major announcement in the budget speech is the devaluation of the Canadian dollar. I am not an economist nor a financier, but I am convinced that the devaluation of the Canadian dollar will increase the cost of living in our country. A great number of foodstuffs that we have to buy daily such as fruits, vegetables, tea, coffee, sugar, etc., are imported, and I am convinced that we shall have to pay more for those products. In addition we have to import a great deal of manufactured products. As another member so rightly stated earlier, some industries have to import from the United States the machinery they require to develop and to replace their equipment.
I am also convinced that the towns, provinces, municipalities, corporations and individuals who borrowed money on the American market and elsewhere will have to pay more for principal and interest, which will mean a supplementary tax for the consumer.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You prefer unemployment.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In his budget speech, the minister stated that he expected a substantial increase in our exports. Well, I hope that prediction will come true, but I am doubtful. Many Canadians are doubtful also, because this is not the first time that the minister makes predictions and his forecasts, in my opinion, are seldom correct.
(Text):
Mr. Speaker, the debate on the budget gives an opportunity to hon. members of this house to speak on a variety of subjects, which in the course of ordinary debate we cannot do. I have been listening for the last four years to many speeches from both sides of this chamber and a number of special words have been used more often than others.
I have no intention of referring to the word "we", which is the most popular word in Hansard, but to more specific words used by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) in his budget speech. In his budget speech the Minister of Finance used the word "vision". When he talked about his expansion policy he said that was a vision which would create greater exportation and bring about more work and more revenue to this country. I hope


that this vision will be better than other visions which were expressed during the campaign of 1957 and 1958 by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and other members of the government.
I know, Mr. Speaker, that there are men of vision. We in the Liberal party are very proud of some of those men of vision we had in the past. Just to name a few I would refer to the Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King. He was a man of vision. The Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent was another. Then there was a great one in the Right Hon. C.
D.	Howe. I was reading just a few weeks ago a speech made by our ex-prime minister, Louis St. Laurent, in which he expressed the view that what is lacking in this government is a man of vision like C. D. Howe.
Another word that was used and which is very familiar to the Minister of Finance is "taxation". In the electoral record of 1957 and 1958 there are many pages of promises to reduce taxation, and today we find that the government is collecting more money than ever in taxation from the Canadian people. So "reduction of taxation" is only a phrase not a fulfilled promise. Then there is "inflation". Well, the minister has always been opposed to inflation and I am opposed to it too. I hope this new devaluation of the Canadian dollar will not bring about inflation.
There is another word, "conversion". We all know what happened with the conversion loan. I believe that the conversion loan is responsible for some of the financial difficulties that the government is in today, because this conversion loan has increased the interest and the government has got to tax the people in order to pay that interest, or mortgage the Canadian people.
"Double depreciation"'-that is a new phrase in Hansard; I have never seen it before this year. It has not brought much result as yet. Let us hope that it will bring results. "Diversion"-this is a word that was very popular in the campaign of 1957 and 1958 when hon. gentlemen opposite were talking about trade. The Conservative members and candidates were then talking about diversion. They were not talking about expansion of trade in those days; no, it was diversion. Well, we know what kind of a result diversion has had in this country.
Then there is the word "expansion". This is a very popular word now. It is the main word in this budget. We will have to wait until the next budget to see whether the meaning the Minister of Finance gives to that word proves to be correct. Then there is the word "confusion". This is a very popular word too, and we know there is confusion. The minister,

in his expose yesterday, said there was confusion between himself and the governor of the Bank of Canada.
Then we have the word "devaluation". This is a new word too. "Devaluation" is another word used in the monetary field, so we will know by next year what this means to this country. "Prediction" is another word. I have talked about predictions. We know all the predictions of the minister and I hope all his predictions, especially one, will come true. I hope his prediction comes true that in two years from now we will have a balanced budget and in three years we will have money with which to start repaying the loans we are obtaining today.
Another very popular word is "consultation". In this debate and previous debates the minister said he had had many consultations with the governor of the Bank of Canada. I had to consult the dictionary to find out what the word "consultation" really means, and according to Webster's dictionary it means conferring for mutual counsel. I am sure the minister has used fully the consultation process with the governor of the Bank of Canada, because when the consultation process breaks down we have another word that comes to my lips and it is "decapitation". Those are some of the words which the Minister of Finance used often in this house.
But there are other words used by other ministers and by members of the government which are also very interesting. There is one I think of readily-"misquotation". I recall a few months ago that the hon. member for St. Denis (Mr. Denis) said to a good many members: why don't you join the club of the misquoted? He said that because almost every day there was a member rising on a question of privilege and saying he had been misquoted.
Another word is "commission". We all know that when the government is in trouble over a problem it appoints a royal commission to settle or delay the problem. Another word is "consideration". It is a very vague word but it is a very useful word for the government. The Prime Minister used it today. Whenever the government is embarrassed by a question asked by the opposition the minister concerned has only to stand up and say: we have this question under serious consideration. Rehabilitation. That is a good word-rehabilitation. When hon. members opposite are speaking of the unemployed people they speak about rehabilitation. There is a good example of rehabilitation in my riding and many of the municipalities have protested. They are going to rehabilitate prisoners from St. Vincent de Paul, Montreal. They will take them to the Gatineau park, about 25 miles from
The Budget-Mr. Best
Ottawa and put them to work. Fortunately they are bringing them into the riding of my hon. friend from Hull (Mr. Caron). They are bringing about 100 criminals there to rehabilitate them but they are depriving local citizens of that work. They have no work for honest workers who have families. There is no need to bring prisoners and place them within 30 miles of Ottawa. I am not against rehabilitating some of these prisoners but why not take them into the Northwest Territories where the government is going to build a railroad? That is where these men would be of use.
"Illusion". Well, there are many illusions and I am sure the government is full of illusions about this budget, but I would not be surprised if the illusion of today proved to be the disillusion of tomorrow. Another word we hear about is "elections". That is an important word. This is the word, this is the subject, and this is the thing that hon. gentlemen opposite believe will get the government and the country out of this mess.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We have heard a number of interesting observations today. Before I make some comments on this budget I should like to congratulate the minister on this lengthy yet meaty item which contained many points of particular interest to my riding as well as points of general interest to many people across Canada. More of that in a moment or so.
The hon. member for Gatineau (Mr. Le-duc) who has just resumed his seat has made a very clever play on words here today. But words are a two-edged sword, I suggest, and I would like to evaluate a few of the words he has mentioned in application to our budget, and his party. The hon. member talks about depreciation and devaluation. I wonder whether we should not apply this in evaluating the Liberal party and its appreciation of our budget here today. The hon. member talked about rehabilitation and I can think of no better use of the term than to apply it to the Liberal party. I think the members of the opposition sitting across the aisle are at this time probably undergoing some form of rehabilitation and perhaps after another two decades or so their rehabilitation will be consummated.
The term confusion has been used and confusion, I suggest, is rampant on that side of the house. It is rampant also, Mr. Speaker, among the group who sit on your immediate left. I would perhaps stretch that further and say even hysteria. I notice a trace of hysteria on that side of the house. Hysteria, I am

The Budget-Mr. Best
told, may amount in a medical sense to illusions of grandeur; in the case of hon. gentlemen opposite, illusions of being elected, or of power. We could go on and on.
The term consultation, a most useful word, has been applied just recently to consultations between the Liberal party and the New Party and, possibly, after the motion by the Ontario young Liberal group, to consultation about the amalgamation of those two parties. This consultation represents temptation, as the hon. member for Gatineau would say- temptation to achieve power by any means whatsoever. This is the way one could apply words of many meaning to different people and to different situations.
Devaluation, a change in the value of the Canadian dollar, is having an important effect on many companies in my riding. In the last few days people in the county of Halton have expressed to me a feeling of certainty that many new export markets will be opened up as a result of this measure. They are very happy about this. They believe that the increased sales they may be able to make as a result of this proposal could lead to further employment and much greater prosperity for the companies and for the region concerned.
I wish, now, to say a few words about the industrial development bank. We have heard of the increased lending figures which have played a part in the story of this bank in the last year or two. The volume of the increase has certainly been proved by the amount of money lent by it to the various companies and businesses throughout Canada. Nevertheless, this recent change, increasing its capital from $160 million to $400 million is a most important move, as is the enlargement of its field of operation to cover virtually all businesses in Canada. The reservation is that organizations such as the farm credit corporation must take precedence before the industrial development bank, particularly with respect to certain specialized types of businesses, such as farming. This increase in the money, the facilities and the scope of the industrial development bank represents a most important move, one of which has been greatly welcomed by people in business all across Canada.
The automobile industry has an effect upon us all. In my riding of Halton we have at Oakville the assembly plant of the Ford Motor Company of Canada. Many thousands of automobile workers live in that area and adjacent ridings. We are hopeful that the dropping of the 7J per cent excise tax on cars will have a marked effect on car sales, with resultant employment in our area. This is a proposal of great importance and one which is welcomed, indeed, by the buying public all across Canada.

In respect to new plant facilities, we were happy, indeed, to note the 50 per cent increase in the rate of capital cost allowance allowed from now on in relation to new assets acquired by businesses, provided it is additional spending over the normal volume in the immediate past. I am sure this will indeed help to speed up reconversion, modernization and expansion of various businesses in our country, and in this regard the government should be congratulated.
It has been my interest while a member of this house, at the meetings of the special committee on research to examine a number of scientific problems which exist in our country, particularly in regard to crown corporations and in the whole field of scientific research in Canada. I think that the provisions in this budget represent an important step toward assisting industries, which are becoming more research conscious, to apply this consciousness and appreciation for increased expenditures in this field in a practical way. Their ability to write off capital expenditures in research not over three years but over a period of one year, is an important advance. I hope this provision will increase research expenditure by various companies.
This type of measure has received the enthusiastic approval of the heads of various corporations including the president of the Ford Motor Company of Canada and others, who have pointed out that they come at a time when industry, government, and the public generally across Canada are becoming much more research conscious.
The lifting of the 5 per cent ceiling on deductible income in respect to research expenditures may enable many firms to spend more in this regard. It has been puzzling to me to decide whether some of these research expenditures have actually been listed under development, expansion or some other heading, but in any case these industries will now be able to give a more accurate fisting of research spending under that heading, now that the ceiling has been lifted.
It is very important also to note that donations to non-profit research foundations will now be deducted from income. This is a matter which has received legal attention recently, and has been given realistic and practical consideration. For instance, in Canada, we have new research foundations such as the Canadian uranium research foundation, sponsored by the various uranium mining companies in this country. This foundation may well conduct research in regard to the methods of processing and alternative uses of the metal uranium, and through its funds it may well let contracts for specific projects to universities or other research organizations. I presume that this projected legislation will

enable such foundations to increase their work, and would enable various trade and industrial groups to set up further foundations to carry out much needed research and development work in Canada. If such a tax provision will enable these groups to carry on this research to a much greater extent, it will prove a most valuable change indeed.
I now come to the specific subject of volunteer firemen. The subject of volunteer firemen has been a very touchy one in my riding. I suggest the problems in connection with this subject commenced in my riding in the town of Oakville and spread to Hamilton and various other sections of southern Ontario. As the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) and his parliamentary secretary will appreciate-

speechtext: The hon. member for Welland (Mr. McMillan) had something to say about that subject.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-this has been a thorny problem indeed. I hear echoes and the wagging of tongues across the way in the distance, Mr. Speaker, but I can't make out the words.
We are very happy to witness the government taking action on this problem and in this regard I should like to congratulate the Minister of Finance and the Minister of National Revenue for their consideration of my case.
Up to $300 may be deducted retroactive to 1958 as expense money paid to various firemen. It has been a very difficult problem for small municipalities, which must provide fire protection services to do so, and the residents of those small municipalities have had to depend upon the loyalty, integrity and ability of the hardworking numerous volunteer firemen. In my riding I would suggest hundreds of individuals are involved. It seems to me a fair and excellent decision to allow money paid to them by way of expenses not to be included as income from now on. This measure is to be retroactive to 1958.

speechtext: Thanks to the hon. member for Welland.

This is not now a contentious matter, but I think the amendment is significant. This bill was introduced in the Senate and a very hot, contentious and earnest fight was conducted there and lost in connection with the name of a company that intends to operate as this company does.
I wish to say that the banking and commerce committee took up this matter. It is not my intention to enlarge upon the evidence that is available by looking at the record of the sittings of the banking and commerce committee with respect to the National Mortgage Corporation of Canada. Complaint was raised earlier, when the bill was introduced in the Senate, with regard to the right of private people to use names such as "national", "Canada" and so on. I indicated that I wished to be brief. I shall therefore simply refer all hon. members of this committee and the people in the country to the record of our proceedings in the banking and commerce committee when we examined this problem.
May I say that I think this was an example of the usefulness of a parliamentary committee. Politics did not enter into the matter at all. If such had been the case, it would not have been possible to change the name of this corporation after protests from Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation which felt that there was some conflict or confusion or some element of difficulty for the public in connection with the name. That crown corporation made the same representations to the Senate. They failed there in getting an amendment.
I simply wish to pay tribute to the general attitude of those who are elected across the country as members of the House of Commons and to refer to the fact that it was felt that no corporation entering into this important field of second mortgages, which is a unique field, was checked to the extent that, as a private enterprise organization, it must use a title that would indicate that it was a private enterprise organization and not a government sponsored organization. This was not a political partisan affair. The suggestion came from members of all parties who attended the meeting of the banking and commerce committee. It was their feeling that corporations, no matter how important their national service might be, must be careful not to use names or appellations that might give rise to confusion in the mind of the public or possibly indicate that they were government sponsored.
