speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I also should like to say a few words on this bill, and to add my condolences to those of the mover of the bill today on
[The Chairman.]
the death of the father of the previous sponsor. We all offer our condolences.
In this bill, as the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River has mentioned, we have seen some of the best operations of this house and of the work of the committee of this house. A great deal of contention was raised in my mind immediately by two events which occurred fairly close together. One was the announcement by the Minister of Public Works that offerings would be made in the secondary mortgage field in relationship with Central Housing and Mortgage Corporation. The second was the advent of this company which had the appearance, because of the name of the company, of being in the mortgage field in competition or of being in the field in such a manner that, because of the name, some difference of opinion would arise whether it was in effect in a field in which we would prefer to see established a crown corporation rather than a private company. The fact that this company has agreed to and the committee has endorsed the idea of changing the name to one more appropriate to a private company and reserving for the crown a name that would of necessity be more acceptable to a crown corporation certainly has been of advantage with regard to the passing of this bill.
In other respects there are many unique factors. One is that we now have a uniform secondary mortgage company that has by law established certain rules and regulations as to its capitalization and to the method of its capitalization. All members of the house, no matter what their political affiliation, I am sure were pleased to note that this company asked that 75 per cent of their directors be Canadian citizens ordinarily resident in Canada. I am sure they were also pleased to note that this company asked for and made part of their bill the requirement that for a period of 15 days at least 60 per cent of any stock offering up to $10 million, with a proposed increase of $5 million to a total of $15 million, would be allowed for sale in Canada to Canadian citizens.
In essence, what does that mean? It means nothing.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration is with us. She would be in a much better position than am I to define what is a Canadian citizen ordinarily resident in Canada. But whatever it is, it sounds fairly good to me. It is a great deal better than we have had in the past.
We have the fact that this company has been established and that there are to be two types of mortgages. The first type is one that can be bought by companies and will be held under trust by this corporation, with a

small payment being made for the management of their bonds. The second type of mortgage will be that in which a number of people can participate, those who wish to do so and who are willing to put their money into second mortgages but who normally would not have enough capital to handle one secondary mortgage. Through its proposals this company has set up the machinery which will allow those people with less than the normal amount of money required for a second mortgage to participate and to take advantage of the opportunity in this field. I think that this bill is an exceptionally good one. I believe it will offer something to the Canadian people, provided that the interest rates are reasonable; and I presume and hope that will be the case as the company have been reasonable in other respects. I believe that this bill will do two things. It will allow the accumulation of the money necessary at the present time for second mortgages, something which will tend to eliminate the very high premium that is now paid on second mortgages, including in many cases an unreasonable bonus. It will also allow people having a limited amount of savings with which to engage in the secondary mortgage field to participate on this basis, with a company that has set up the machinery that will protect the investment they care to make under this legislation.

Mr. Chairman, I believe the bill now before the committee is rather unique and I should like to say a few words about it. In the first place, I heartily endorse the amendment that has been proposed. I do believe that we must be-and we have not always been-very cautious before we authorize the use by Canadian companies of such words as "national", "royal" or "dominion" in their name. Equally so, I believe that a company incorporated in the province of Ontario carrying in its name the word "Ontario" operates at unfair advantage over other companies. A company incorporated in British Columbia ought not to be permitted to use in the name of the company the words "British Columbia". I say this because to the average, innocent Canadian there is the implication that this particular company might have the backing of either the province or the nation. Therefore I want to compliment the committee for proposing the amendment that is now before us, that the word "national" be eliminated and another word be substituted for it.
We have long asked for action on the part of the government to eliminate the racketeering that exists in the sale of mortgage paper in Canada. Several months ago the government announced its intention of moving in this direction in that C.M.H.C. was going to
Private Bills
place on the market blocks of half a million dollars each of real estate paper. As I understand it, this company is specifically designed in order to take advantage of these potential offerings of the government. I would like to heartily congratulate the company for many aspects of its articles of incorporation as they now appear before the committee. In the first place I notice that the shares are going to be offered in denominations of $10 each. I would advise any Canadian with idle investment capital, no matter how small, to participate in an effort of this kind. I believe this is a bona fide-
Is this what you are recommending?
Yes, the money will be invested in insured mortgages.
You are recommending investment in fixed securities rather than in equities, in a period of inflation. Did you not hear the budget?

I am not going to discuss inflation at the moment. I believe this is a bona fide Canadian corporation and they realize the possibilities that exist in this field of buying and selling mortgages on real estate. I would also like to endorse the commendations made by the hon. member for Timiska-ming. I notice that this company insists that not less than 75 per cent of its directors shall at all times be Canadian citizens ordinarily resident in Canada.
I also like another aspect of this matter, whereby before there will be any offerings of the stock of the company on the world market Canadians will be given at least a 15-day leeway in which to participate. I realize at once that this is only one of many hundreds of Canadian companies and corporations which will be eligible to submit bids on offerings of mortgage paper by C.M.H.C. and to deal in other types of mortgage paper. However, I believe this is the first time this parliament has been asked to incorporate a company that is basically a Canadian company in concept and also in its intentions as to manner of operation.
Nonsense. Anybody can buy stock in this company.
Carried.

Mr. Chairman, having heard the remarks of the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam I feel obliged to say a few words on this matter. I am not opposing the incorporation of this company, because countless companies based on principles similar to those enunciated in this bill have been incorporated by this parliament. However, when federal incorporation is required, as a

Private Bills
member of parliament I think I should warn my colleagues that it is just wishful thinking to believe that some of the clauses in this bill are different than those in bills incorporating other mortgage corporations.
The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam referred to the fact that 75 per cent of the directors must be Canadian. To me that means nothing. It is a question of whether or not the directors are truly owners of the stock in the company, or whether they are simply nominees of foreign holders of stock in the company.
To me several clauses in this bill are simply window dressing, eyewash and nonsense in so far as any drive on our part is concerned for effective, proper legislative control to reduce foreign ownership. I said at the beginning of my remarks that I am not opposing the bill, but I do not like the eyewash and the suggestion that this is a good measure because 15 days are given as an opportunity for subscription for stock. In my opinion that means nothing, in connection with the National Mortgage Corporation of Canada.
In my opinion dummy residents in Canada could subscribe for stock within that 15-day limit, and realistically it has nothing whatever to do with the terms of this bill. I am not opposing the bill, because we have approved bills of this kind for a long time; but I do want to indicate that we are not being misled in any way that this is more of a "Canadianization" bill than any other bill of this kind which has been presented to parliament for federal legislation.
It is more Canadian than is Aurora.

I think perhaps similar faults prevail in both cases. I am saying that the technical devices, the legal devices applied to invoke the principles that might be in the minds of all hon. members of this parliament when we think of Canadianization are really, if we look at this bill, completely defeated by reason of the fact that 15 days after the opportunity for Canadians to buy, a United States or foreign investor could buy through a dummy Canadian citizen. I simply want to warn other applicants for incorporation that we in parliament are not so stupid about our wishes with regard to incorporation and Canadian ownership that we think if they put some of the meaningless clauses into a private bill such window dressing enhances its likehood of passing through the House of Commons.
I say I intend to vote for the bill because we have not voted against similar bills in the past, but I am not for a moment misled about the appointment of directors or the

offering of stock for 15 days to Canadians. I am not misled for a moment into thinking this necessarily means the Canadian ownership and operation of this company in the future.

This question is obviously of great interest to the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River. I think I do not have the same appreciation of Canadians he has. I cannot apply the word dummy to them, not to all of them, at any rate. Of course, when one looks across to the other side of the chamber the word may come to mind.
I think that perhaps in essence what the hon. member says is true, namely, that the intent set out here could be subverted. That is correct, but that is no reason for not adhering to the principle and the hope, barring any international barriers placed around the country which prevent the movement back and forth of people and money. Barring these things I do not think we shall ever be able to develop any legislation, which will be completely effective along these lines.
I am not opposing this bill but I do not want parliament to be kidded by this clause.

I appreciate that. I think I have the same appreciation as the hon. member does of the effect of this. I realize the intent and the purpose of this could be destroyed very easily by the company itself, as far as that goes, and also by others who have an interest in it and who want to act on behalf of individuals who have money outside the country. I think this would be true in all instances. But it is no reason for us to sit back and do nothing about it. I think we should consciously attempt to promote Canadian ownership of corporations just as we should consciously attempt to promote Canadian control of another company whose affairs may come up 'for discussion following this.

I cannot lightly pass by the warning issued by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River. The hon. member called this particular aspect of the bill nonsense and mere window dressing. However, if I understand this matter rightly, if I own some equity in a Canadian corporation and if I attend the annual meeting I am able to cast votes according to the equity I hold. If I have
5,000	shares I am able to cast 5,000 votes while another man, who may have only 11 shares, can cast only 11 votes. However, this does not apply once you have been elected to the board of directors. I have never yet heard of a board of directors where the vote of one director counts for more than the vote of another director and if this bill says that not

less than 75 per cent of the directors must be bona fide Canadians I cannot understand why the hon. member should call that nonsense and window dressing.
A director could be a dummy if he was appointed to the board because somebody else in the United1 States could own 75 per cent of the stock.

I appreciate that. Yet there is in the hearts of Canadians, I hope, such a thing as loyalty to their nation. I can well imagine that the recent rumpus we had over the unloading of grain that we sold to China or the rumpus we had some years ago over the issue raised by the hon. member for Vancouver East when the sale of rubber belts or conveyor belts to China was blocked would never have happened if 75 per cent of those who had the right to cast a vote had been Canadians basically.
In 1958 in connection with Ford products they got their orders from Detroit.

I know there may be Canadians who will subvert the national interest for their own selfish interest. I know nothing at all about the men who are responsible basically for the organization of this company. However, I have reason to believe they are bona fide Canadians and I would much prefer to support the incorporation of a company of this kind than to support, as we are often asked to do in this house, a company being organized by a legal firm which we know is acting on behalf of outside financial interests. I am sure even the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River is happy to know that the men responsible for the sponsoring of this bill are not merely a smokescreen for the Household Finance Corporation, for instance, which is a United States interest.
I hope not.

There may be some merit in what the hon. member has said. He has attempted to warn the house that we ought not to be misled, that our intentions can be frustrated despite the terms of this bill. However, I believe the expressions contained in this bill will have a beneficial result on our national interest because I think that in the years to come we shall see more and more incorporations including clauses along these lines, and despite any dirty work that may go on behind the scenes at times I think the long range intention is good and that it will have a good effect.

Having heard the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam I shall say very tersely that I agree in large part. I will only repeat that the clauses of the bill in

It will be noted in this clause the petitioners are seeking to incorporate this company under the name The Acadia Life Insurance Company, and in French, L'Acadia Compagnie d'Assurance-Vie herein after called "the company".
The point I wish to make is that this follows the desirable practice which has been adopted by the house of granting alternative names to companies incorporated by special act. Under our Companies Act, companies seeking incorporation by letters patent do not have the same right and can only take a name in one or other language. This fact presents a great deal of difficulty to national companies which do business in all sections of Canada who have to use a name in a language which may not be used in a particular section of the country. I have reason to suspect that there are many companies, and some I know for certain, which would prefer to have alternative names for use in different parts of the country. I can see no objection at all to the same practice being used under the Companies Act as is used in these special acts of incorporation provided the translation of the name is carefully done. subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The house resumed consideration of the motion of Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Benidickson.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Before dinner, Mr. Speaker, I was discussing some of the measures introduced by our recent budget and the particular effect they have on the various groups of people in my riding. These measures, such as the one with respect to our dollar, writeoffs in respect of capital expenditures in various fields, new provisions for new plant facilities and research expenditures, are measures which I am sure will please and affect many areas of our country.
I was drawing attention to the fact that two particular measures play an important part in my riding and before their implementation I had discussed these at some length with the ministers of the departments involved. The provision in respect of payments to volunteer firemen is one such measure, and the matter of a duty or tariff on chicken imports from the United States is another. This latter matter is one which will affect many specialized farmers, broiler growers, those who produce eggs and, indeed, the whole chicken industry. There are many hundreds of these specialized farmers in my riding and in adjacent ridings. They have for a long time wanted some equality of duty or tariff on fowl coming into Canada with our own exports to the United States. This measure introduced by the government has been warmly greeted by people in the riding of Halton who are concerned with this business. This duty of five cents per pound on eviscerated chicken, will apply to cut up and cooked chicken as well, and will thus be important to our broiler growers and all people associated with the poultry industry.
There are other budget measures which we could discuss this evening if time permitted, such as the complex financial matters which will have a profound effect over the weeks and months on various sections of Canada. The opposition, as voiced by some members of the Liberal party and the C.C.F. party, has been particularly weak in the days succeeding the introduction of the budget. The opposition has been lengthy but rather empty of content, I would suggest, as is the Liberal 90205-6-152
The Budget-Mr. Best
amendment itself, which mentions trade restrictions and so forth. I feel that the measures introduced may not really be restrictive of trade at all. Indeed, they may stimulate a great increase in our export trade. I believe the total effect of these measures upon our country will be beneficial, particularly to our export trade.
In considering the various opposition speakers, most of whom are not here tonight, I would say it has been noted in recent days that the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillin-gate (Mr. Pickersgill) has demonstrated a mounting, increasing hysteria as evidenced by the volume and loudness of his attacks on the government. We all realize that the session has been long and perhaps the hon. member for his own sake could stand a good rest and a bit of refreshment before he continues mounting these attacks in this house. We were very much interested in his comments just a few days ago and the fact that he does not read a high proportion of the letters he receives. I think that few of us could say that we read absolutely everything. Most of us try to read all of our correspondence. An admission of this sort by a former Liberal cabinet minister but now a private member, is a most interesting one indeed.
Perhaps I can continue in relation to the tariff measure on chickens that I was discussing previously and note his off-hand reference to gutless chickens, as he put it. If this indicates the importance attached to this matter by the hon. member and indeed by the Liberal party, it is something of which I feel the farmers of Canada ought to take note in a very serious degree. We cannot blame them too much on the opposition side, however, since the position of farm or agricultural critic seems to be constantly shifting around among a variety of members on that side of the house.
The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillin-gate in a previous debate in this budget set of speeches mentioned something about "off with the heads" of senior civil servants in this country. I do not think the people of our country have any thought whatsoever that any action which the government is now taking in reference to the Bank of Canada means this sort of thing at all. As a matter of fact, in my own opinion and in that of most of the constituents from whom I have heard, we have really leaned over backwards to be fair, honest and, if at all possible, accommodating with respect to the governor of the Bank of Canada. The same thing may be said with respect to other senior people in public life. I think we have been extremely fair in this matter. I would suggest to the

The Budget-Mr. Best
Liberal members that they look into their own background in this field before casting such aspersions at others.
I mentioned agricultural matters. It was rather interesting to see in recent days the trespassing by various other members of the Liberal party in this field which I had come to think belonged to the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin). The hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith), for instance, got into the grain trade business in recent days. The hon. member for Niagara Falls (Miss LaMarsh) commented rather plaintively on matters of drought and grasshoppers in the west. Indeed, today the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) got into the cattle market, perhaps to his subsequent sorrow. This business of an agriculture shadow cabinet minister has really been travelling the circuit in the Liberal party opposite. I am sorry the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson) is not here this evening as he was so much in evidence this afternoon. Perhaps we should congratulate him in that he seems to have maintained his shadow or shadowy position of opposition financial critic.
The hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer) in this budget debate a few days ago commented on various topics. He suggested that we have cut down on various important works in this country. When this procedure was necessary and when it seemed wise, we have indeed done so. But, Mr. Speaker, I would call to your attention and to that of the people of this country the tremendous increase of funds, and the building and construction in general which has taken place in the last three or four years. I could name hospitals, roads, dams, house construction, public building construction, airports and so on, a whole long string of projects, which this government has fostered to an increasing extent and which really negate and deny any such argument on the part of the hon. member for Trinity.
But this hon. gentleman a few days ago, as found at page 6888 of Hansard, mentioned that if the government took itself seriously it would realize that these skills must start at the top, and that we must have a skilled government. By inference I presume he meant that a skilled government could arise from the members sitting opposite us. This is a rather ludicrous thought. We may have seen, of course, in recent weeks prior to the byelections at least, I suppose fully half of the members of the Liberal opposition counting on various cabinet positions for themselves. We can see this subtle build-up and we can see the much more sudden deflation following the by-elections which they won in the proportion of one out of four. Hence if a

skilled government is necessary, Mr. Speaker, I submit that we have it now; and I submit that the alternatives on the other side of this house are simply not in existence at the present time.
The hon. member for Niagara Falls, in discussing the budget, talked about various problems out west, as I said before and I think really typified, along with others, the sort of mounting hysteria which we have noticed in the opposition party. The obvious divisions within this party about which we hear in private and which are frequently exemplified in public, are ones which will have to be worked out in the period of years that follow.
I observe my friend the hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Pitman) sitting down at the far end of the chamber. We were interested in his comments on the budget as well. With regard to some of the very interesting remarks he made, I think we could agree with him. I note the comments which the hon. member for Peterborough made, as found at page 6895 of Hansard where he states:
Indeed, there are few extreme positions; life is nothing but finding compromises.
I suggest that this is not the spirit of a New party member. While it may be a wise personal decision on the part of the hon. member for Peterborough, I am sure he must be suffering acute indigestion in the group in which he finds himself at the moment. I would rather agree with his position, but it is not the philosophical position of the incipient party to which he belongs.
Then we go on to the hon. gentleman's other comments about this country perhaps becoming a banana republic and so on. I believe there is instance after instance in which this government has asserted in a true and independent spirit our differences with the country to the south of us, our great friendship with it but our distinct differences. It has taken a government such as that which we have had in the last four years to assert these differences, to stand up from a position of honesty and strength in various difficult and individual positions which have fallen upon us. In short, Mr. Speaker, I cannot accept the long and frequently windy but completely vacant and empty opposition which has come to the present budget. We do not pretend to say that it has solved all our problems but it has made major steps in many directions.
I cannot sit down without one final comment on these various remarks from the two opposition parties. We have talked about various types of fowl, farm problems and a number of miscellaneous items. One which came to my attention just a few days ago

involved a mouse and a tiger. This mouse and tiger combination is one which I think may ring down the succeeding months and years with loud reverberations. When the president of the Liberal association of Ontario describes the approach of his party to the incipient New Party as a mouse coming to a tiger, I think perhaps half of that description at least is correct. I would not say that about the whole of it. But I welcome with an open heart the honesty of this man in voicing his opinion and his true feelings, and we are glad indeed that it has come to the public's notice in recent days.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the reason members of the government in power did not speak on the budget before today is no doubt due to the fact that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) put them to sleep when he made his marathon speech on budget night. They woke up suddenly today. We had nearly three hours of words, words, words-30,000 of them-when the whole thing could have been said in one hour at the most. I have never heard the Minister of Finance make a speech so uninteresting, so devoid of interest as was the budget speech. Of course a budget that offered so little had to be couched in many words. I have great respect for the Minister of Finance, but he certainly disappointed me on budget night. The Canadian public soon realized that this was again a deficit budget, in which the Minister of Finance specializes, and soon lost interest. It made me think of the old saying: You may fool all the people some of the time; you can even fool some of the people all the time; but you cannot fool all of the people all the time.
Mr. Speaker, may I quote from a Montreal financial weekly under the date June 22, 1961. E. J. DeSeau, the financial editor had this to say. It is a long article and I will not read it all:
The budget was not worth delay. Not even size of cash deficit offered any new surprise.
The article continues:
The platitudinous preambles to the budget were undoubtedly spoken in Donald Fleming's voice but the words were those of the Prime Minister.
This is clearly a government by fall guys.
We would say that nobody really knows who is next in line for some sort of misery. But what matters at this moment is this budget.
Was it worth being delayed from April till June? It was not.
Is it an expansionist budget?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

May I, Mr. Speaker, read from the annual address of Mr. W. Earle McLaughlin, president of the Royal Bank of Canada.
It is time we stopped talking dangerous nonsense about using fiscal and monetary policy, not for their legitimate purposes, but as an allegedly "easy" way of bringing down the exchange rate or the interest rate, or both. I should now like to quote from a Montreal newspaper of Monday, November 14, 1960:
U.S. investment brings more good than harm.

The article continues:
"It was United States capital that opened the iron fields of Labrador and Steep Rock, the nickel deposits in Manitoba and to a large extent the petroleum and natural gas resources of the west."
From 1931 to 1935 inclusively, under a Conservative regime Canada had a yearly deficit. This deficit, for the five years under a Conservative regime as I stated previously, totalled $668,346,999. From 1947 to 1956 inclusively, under a Liberal regime Canada had a total surplus, not a deficit, of $2,120,537,800.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We will probably beat that this year.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Tory years are always depression years. "Deficit Don" has done it again. The minister will depend on, and no doubt will hope, for a lowering of the interest rates in Canada. How this is to be done was not clearly explained in the budget speech. The effect will be to make investments in Canada less attractive to foreign lenders. It has been said that this government will have to borrow an average of $100 million a month for the balance of the fiscal year to meet the estimated cash deficit of $650 million. It is anticipated that the expenditures for 1961 will be $6,415,000,000, and the anticipated revenue is $5,961,000,000. The Minister of Finance and this Tory government have added $2,056,000,000 to Canada's public debt in four years.
Mr. Speaker, may I read from Labor, a weekly publication, issue of Saturday, March 25, 1961:
Business failures jump in Canada.
Business failures increased 21 per cent between 1959 and 1960, according to the dominion bureau of statistics. Defaulted liabilities under the provisions of the bankruptcy and winding up acts reached $148,253,000. The increase in business failures were substantial in general merchandising, auto products, building materials as well as in iron and steel and wood products manufacturing industries.
The high taxation with which industry is saddled is stinting our competitive ability. The government should realize how badly off industry is in comparison with most of our foreign competitors. Gross corporate earnings are taxed at a flat 50 per cent rate. No distinction is made between what is distributed and what is ploughed back into the company to provide for expansion, thereby enabling it to manufacture a cheaper, better and more competitive product.
Canadian industry is allowed less favourable depreciation rates than most of its foreign competitors. Under our tax laws, not much more than 20 per cent of the cost of a piece of equipment having a 15-year life can be written off in the first year. Britain and Japan permit a first year write-off of about 50 per cent; Sweden, 40 per cent and Italy more than 30 per cent.
The United Kingdom provides many other exemptions such as 20 per cent on new machinery and plant in the year of acquisition deductible from taxable income. This is in addition to the regular depreciation on machinery which would amount to approximately 15 per cent plus an extra initial


allowance of 10 per cent in the first year. This government should take a leaf out of the Britishers' book in this matter of investment allowance. Semi and fully manufactured products account for more than one third of all the export dollars we earn in any given year. The last final figures available are those of 1959. They show that such goods brought us in $1,860 million, or 37 per cent of the total income from the export of Canadian products in that year. Our 1959 purchases abroad of fully manufactured goods, were equal to $244 for every man, woman and child in Canada.
The amount spent by Canadians for competitive imports is little short of fantastic. Individual Canadians bought 4.7 times as much fully manufactured goods as did the Britishers in 1959, nearly 4.9 times as much as the west Germans, 6.4 times as much as the Americans and 27 times as much as the Japanese. We have a favourable trade balance with European nations and a heavy adverse balance with the U.S.A. How long will European nations continue to pay for our luxurious imports from the U.S.A.?
One thing is sure to result from this budget. The cost of living will rise as our dollar declines. We have a serious unemployment problem but it is as nothing compared with what this problem will be unless we take immediate measures to check the uncontrolled flow of printed matter from foreign countries and principally from the United States. Our small population in Canada is called upon to support the greatest volume of imported printing of any country in the world. Sixty per cent of United States printing exports are absorbed by Canada. Only 5 per cent of our printing exports are absorbed by the United States. The population of the United States is approximately 180 million. Canada's population is about one-tenth of that. For every rabbit we sell to the United States we have to purchase 12 elephants. This applies to the printing industry only. Possibly similar comparisons can be made in other industries.
Printed imports to Canada from the United States and all other countries for the year 1953 amounted to $130,679,553, as compared with $183,716,509 for 1959, which represents an increase of $53,036,956. Printed exports shipped from Canada to the United States and all other countries for the year 1953 amounted to $5,451,234 as compared with $8,927,732 for 1959, which is an increase of $2,994,038. Let us compare the difference. In 1959, Canada imported from the United States and all other countries printed matter to the value of $183,716,509 and in the same year the total Canadian exports were

The Budget-Mr. Bourque
$8,927,732, representing an imbalance between exports and imports of $174,788,777.
I understand that a group of officials was sent to Europe recently where they visited Her Majesty's stationer in England and some of the leading European industrialists. Though I cannot vouch for this, my information is that in England they were looking into the possibility of Her Majesty's printer doing some printing for the government of Canada, and that they were also looking for information about British government printing operations in order to justify our own printing bureau to the Glassco commission. I also believe that this delegation visited the Olivetti company in Italy. What was the reason for this delegation? Is the government thinking of importing more printed matter from Great Britain and other European countries, thereby increasing unemployment in the graphic industries in Canada?
We are now experiencing the influx into the labour force of many tens of thousands of young Canadians, those born after the end of the second world war. Industry will have to absorb a large proportion of these if we are not to be faced with chronic unemployment. The planning to put an end to unemployment must be undertaken right now. Too long has this government been dilly-dallying with this problem. It will be too late and worse than useless to be throwing up our hands in consternation five years from now. The government should confer immediately with industry, labour, educators and parents in order to prepare the way to put to work every single one of these young Canadians. They must be trained, however, so that they will possess the knowledge, intelligence and skills that industry needs and must have in these difficult times.

In a period of serious unemployment there are many thousands of jobs going begging in Canada today for no other reason than that there are too few people with the necessary education and technical qualifications to fill them.
Long enough has this government dodged its responsibilities. It should invest in the training of such people rather than continue indefinitely to help them in uneducated idleness draining the unemployment insurance fund dry, or subsisting on government relief.
I have gleaned much of my information from the address given by the president of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association at its ninth annual general meeting. The unemployment insurance fund sank to $110,051,922 at May 31, the lowest point since its building era. A year ago the fund was at $299,293,000, and at April 30 this year it stood at $143,651,000. The $33 million dip in May was one of the sharpest May declines in the fund's 20 year history.
Municipalities could play an important part in restoring and maintaining full employment. For this purpose large sums of capital would be required at interest rates which the local communities could afford. Most Canadian municipalities have reached the limit of their borrowing power. They are forced to compete in the financial market with the more attractive securities of the dominion and the provinces making municipal borrowings practically impossible.
If the federal government created a national development fund to assist municipalities in financing improvements in public services and utilities at a reasonably low interest rate, this would create jobs for thousands of unemployed throughout Canada. Unless immediate measures are taken to get the unemployed back in jobs Canada faces the unenviable prospect of continued unemployment and a grim future of poverty and dire misery.
Since 1956 approximately 41,000 employees have been dropped by the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway. These figures relate to one type of industry only. We are told the railways are losing money, their losses are increasing every year. If their earnings do not increase we can expect to have further curtailment of railroad services. Chances of any increase in the passenger or freight traffic do not look very bright. Let us put back to work the 625,000 unemployed persons in Canada and soon the goods manufactured by these people will keep traffic moving at a rapid pace. We must set to work right now, resolved to find a solution to our problems.

The Budget-Mr. Bourque Mr. Bourque: The Canadian market is saturated with Japanese goods. Most of these goods should and could be manufactured right here in Canada which would give employment to thousands upon thousands of our unemployed. The textile industry has been greatly affected by our purchases of Japanese goods. Japanese shipments of clothing, textile products and fabrics to this country totalled $40,200,000 in 1960 and $41,500,000 in 1959 as compared with $5 million in 1954. The textile workers union of America recently wired the Minister of Finance pointing out that 35,000 Canadian textile workers had lost their jobs. They demanded immediate government action to curb the flood of imports. In 1951 the textile industry employed
102,000	Canadians and produced 75 per cent of the textiles sold in Canada. They now produce 48 per cent to 52 per cent of the market and employ about 70,000. In the first seven months of 1960 Japan exported to Canada a total of 3,220,000 square yards of man made fabrics against 3,411,000 square yards for the whole of 1959 and 1,049,000 square yards for all of 1958. Based on the above figures, Canada will have absorbed more of these goods in 1960 than in the two previous years.
I should now like to quote from an article by John Meyer which appeared in the Montreal Gazette of April 14, 1961:
The Japanese argument for continued access to the Canadian market on their terms is, heaven knows, familiar enough. The Japanese buy more from us than they sell; they insist that the only fair trade is a balanced trade. They buy a million dollars worth of our goods; we buy a million dollars worth of their goods. The economics of such a contention, if fully applied, would bankrupt Canada in short order. The products we sell to Japan create jobs; the products we buy from Japan destroy jobs.
I have touched only on the textile industry but, apply the same thing to all our industries and you will soon realize what the principal cause of our unemployment problem is.
"Japan Today" written by Christopher M. Young, Southam news correspondent supplies the following information:
Ninety three million people occupy a land area slightly smaller than the province of Newfoundland where fewer than half a million people live. The busy millions of Japan provide a ravenous domestic market for the products of industry. Despite its huge domestic market, Japan depends for its prosperity on its sales abroad. Its own national resources are limited.
To manufacture in quantity and to feed its people, Japan must buy heavily abroad. To pay for these imports, it must sell heavily abroad.
Japan's markets today are North America, southeast Asia, Africa and Europe in that order. Ninety three million people in a land the size of a small Canadian province simply cannot survive without trade.
We do not want the Japanese to starve but if we import more of their goods Canadians will be threatened not only with 
increased unemployment but also with starvation. The government must take proper measures to increase available jobs for Canadians and thereby decrease unemployment.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had no intention of taking part in the budget debate but considering the lack of sincerity displayed by the Liberals and the complaints they made, I have decided to show the other side of the picture.
Since the beginning of the budget debate, we have heard members of the opposition complaining that the Conservative government never presents anything but deficits. Yet, during the campaign which preceded the last by-elections, we heard none other than the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) urgently call for deficit budgeting. That is an example of the inconsistency and lack of sincerity of the Liberals. The only thing they are interested in is power, and ever since they have been removed from power, they have not stopped whining. It has become an obsession with them to be in the opposition.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I think they should get used to it because as far as the people of Canada are concerned, they are going to stay there for a long while.
Another very convincing proof of their lack of sincerity is that in the same breath they proclaim themselves leaders in the field of social justice and think of themselves as champions because they have introduced the Unemployment Insurance Act, while at the same time they deplore that Canadian workers are deprived of unemployment insurance benefits.
That is a sure sign of their lack of sincerity. It goes to prove that when they introduced unemployment insurance, they did it merely with a view to extorting money from the workers, because they had no intention whatsoever that the workers should benefit from that legislation. They complain now that workers are taking advantage of the Unemployment Insurance Act that we, Conservatives, have improved and will keep on improving. Let our good friends opposite shed tears and whine. I can understand that after spending 21 years in power they can hardly get used to being in the opposition.
Mr. Speaker, I will only take a few moments to show the other side of the picture. The two Liberal members who spoke before me contended that bankruptcies were increasing under the Conservatives. Well, let us see what the real situation is. I have here Le Devoir of Tuesday June 27, 1961. Here is what I read on page 10:
In the first quarter of 1961, commercial bankruptcies under the Bankruptcy Act and liquidations
The Budget-Mr. Ricard
numbered 729, which means 3.8 per cent less than the 758 a year earlier, whereas liabilities dropped considerably from $78,495,000 to $26,999,000. Average liabilities per bankruptcy were $37,000, compared to $103,600 a year earlier.
However, that will not stop the lamentations of the opposition-they contend that bankruptcies are on the increase in Canada, while the contrary is rather the case.

On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, I dislike interrupting the hon. gentleman, who normally makes a very effective contribution to debate in the house, but I think he is now infringing the rule. The hon. member is quoting from newspapers which are reflecting upon proceedings within the house, and he is doing this for the purpose of attempting to influence decision in the course of debate here in the House of Commons.
In Beauchesne's fourth edition, on page 133, there are two citations which I think are worth considering. In citation 157, subsection 5, Beauehesne says:
It is not in order to read articles in newspapers, letters or communications emanating from persons outside the house and referring to, or commenting on, or denying anything said by a member or expressing any opinion reflecting on proceedings within the house.
Subsection 6 reads:
On the 17th March, 1933, a member quoting a newspaper in debate was ruled out of order by the Deputy Speaker who said: "The rule is quite clear, that the quoting of a newspaper, an author or a book which reflects upon debate before the house, either directly or indirectly is entirely out of order, because members are here to give their own opinion and not to quote the opinion of

The Budget-Mr. M. Martin others... Members may quote an article or a book stating facts, but a commentary on any proceeding or any discussion in the house, with the object of swinging an opinion to one side or the other, is out of order".
I think the hon. member who has been addressing the house has been using these quotations from newspapers in order to attempt to affect opinion here in the course of debate. I suggest to you, sir, that according to the rules the hon. member is out of order.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
May I say, Mr. Speaker, that the quotations I have been reading are a reflection of my own ideas, and although I may have found them in a newspaper they none the less correspond completely with my own thoughts, particularly what one prominent newspaper had to say. It went something like this, that we are still in an era of improvisation and groping. There was another article which I believed described the situation very well and the headline, as I recall it, was to the effect: "Too little, because too late". It suggested, as we have suggested so often in this house, that by the time this government gets around to applying a measure to solve some situation, unfortunately the situation that it is trying to solve is some 20 years old and a whole new list of problems has grown up in the meantime.


The Globe and Mail, that good old friend of the Conservative party, after offering some mild criticism, went on to agree completely with the government. I hope the minister does not take any objection to that. It pointed out that the minister had emphasized the need to maintain at all costs the good old private enterprise system and added that the minister had listed a number of worth-while measures which the government intended to take. For example, they were going to increase the depreciation allowance for business; there were three or four different measures they were going to adopt in order to bolster industry and business, and the reason for this was because it had been requested for a long time. But there are also many other things which have been requested for a long time; I do not see them in this budget and I do not think anybody else can see them either. For example, for a long time people have been recommending a decrease in income tax or, possibly, an increase in exemptions under the Income Tax Act. I fail to find anything of that nature in the budget. The same thing applies as far as the sales tax is concerned, a tax which affects each and every individual regardless of his circumstances. The unemployed have been looking for jobs for a long time, now. But there is nothing in this budget to indicate that they are not going to continue to look in vain.
Nevertheless, there is one thing we can find in this budget. We have noticed it already. The old age pensioners have something to look forward to in this budget, and it is not an increase in their pension. It is an increase in their cost of living brought about by the measures taken by this government.
What are these Tory measures? What are these measures which the minister advocates and which receive so much praise in the Tory newspapers? Well, it follows the good old Tory policy that the only solution they can find is to try to help business, to let the "haves" get away with more and more. As a result, we shall have to soak the "have nots" to make up for it. What amazes me is that both the minister and this government and the Tory newspapers go blindly along this road completely ignoring the fact that they have been trying these measures for 94 years and that is what has gotten us in the mess we are in today. I do not know how many times they will have to be shown this before it will ever sink into their heads.
I wish, Mr. Speaker, that I had the time and the facilities to tally up the measures passed by this government in the last four years and see how many of those measures were designed to prop up business and how many were in the interest of the individual taxpayer. I think it would be an impressive

score. It seems strange to me that this government cannot understand that there are only two ways in which we can run a country. One is to raise enough money to do it and the other is to borrow enough money to do it. Apparently this government has decided that the only way they can accomplish it is by the second way. They refuse to do it the first way but they adopt the second solely for the reason that by doing so they can fool the public for a little while longer.
There is one bright side to our economy today, and only one that I can see. That is housing, the bright spot in the building industry. It is interesting to find out just why. We find that in an article by Farrell Crook in the Globe and Mail of today. We find that activity in the over-all construction industry is up some 16 per cent compared with the same period in 1960. Why is it up 16 per cent? We find that the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation reports that in the first five months of this year starts were made on 29,337 dwelling units in centres of more than
5,000	population, a jump of 40.7 per cent compared with last year. So it took a 40.7 per cent jump under this socialistic measure to give us a 16 per cent increase in our over-all picture. If we look through further we find out again why-it was because the free enterprise part of our construction industry, according to contract awards, is down 30 per cent as compared with last year. It makes me wonder just how long this self-illusion on the part of this government can be maintained; how long they can hang on to the idea which is propounded by the Prime Minister in his clarion call that the next election should be fought on the issue of free enterprise versus socialism.
Bad as the situation has been, I wonder whether the government has stopped for one moment to think what the situation would have been like over the last three years if it had not been for our old age pensions, our old age security payments, our blind and disabled pensions, our veterans pensions, family allowances and unemployment insurance, building and construction under the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, our industrial development bank, our much lauded winter works program, our home improvement loans and public works department construction? Had it not been for all these measures-measures which I do not think anyone by any stretch of the imagination could call free enterprise measures-we should be back exactly where we were in the early thirties. Our country would be in chaos.
I think it is interesting to note what the Economist of London has to say about the over-all situation in Canada. I should like to quote from an editorial which appeared in
The Budget

Mr. M. Martin the Toronto Daily Star of June 3, 1961 entitled "Plan for Growth" which reads as follows:
One of the western world's most authoritative and respected publications, the Economist of London, says Canada faces a bleak decade unless it reexamines its ineffective economic policy and begins to plan for something better.

The contrast between this limited function and those employed elsewhere is startling. Whether in Europe's "common market" or in the Red bloc, planning is a vital fact of economic life. The editorial continues, as follows:
If we as a nation are to grow and prosper; if we are to adjust our efforts to the conditions in the new and thoroughly planned world, we ourselves better begin planning.-For, as the Economist suggests, the alternative is continued decay.

Hon. members opposite were given full scope and while they have filled many pages we are not much wiser even now. Frankly, Mr. Speaker, the reason is that the Liberal party is at sixes and sevens in its attitude toward the budget. Fury and storm have been promised, a real side-raking, slashing attack, but apart from the exhibition put on by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) there has been none of that fury and storm.
We did see a frenzied and, I would add, rather frantic performance by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate exceeded only

in slight degree by that incredible speech of last night in another debate. Had he not been suffering from a bad case of foot-in-mouth disease, and we have heard the reference to gutless chickens and his confessions about letters from constituents and elsewhere, we would have thought that he was putting on a display of histrionics in competition with the dramatic festival of much greater note and worth at Stratford at this time.
However, the prerogative of putting on that great dramatic show is reserved for his running mate, the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin), as he thunders away, as he postulates and postures, as he plays to the gallery, always in mock indignation oblivious of all but the self-intoxicating volume of his own exuberance.
But other than these minor blows there has been none of that fighting attitude that had been announced with such fanfare and such ballyhoo and, as we know now, such false bravado last January. That bravado has been displayed from time to time since then but, Mr. Speaker, there is a curious parallel between 1961 and 1958. In 1958 there was a conclave in January. To the sound of trumpets and a great to-do the Liberals came up posturing for a fight. There was a great thumping of chests, cries of bring on the lions, and after a violent travail those of us who were here in January, 1958 saw the Liberals give birth to a puny runt of a mouse. How the people of Canada reacted to that mouse was well recorded some two months later.
Again in 1961 we have had the sound and fury, the January conclave, the trumpets and the ballyhoo, the threatening growls and, quite in keeping, the puny runt of a mouse. That mouse is the amendment put forward by the genial member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson) as financial critic for the official opposition. Not for a moment do I believe that the hon. member is the author of that amendment. He certainly was not the author of that other notorious and unlamented-by the Liberals-amendment of January, 1958. We rather know who was the author or at least the inspiration for that one. I would say the same for the present amendment. That busy, busy man of the Liberal party I think was not too far away when the present amendment was concocted.
I had some other remarks about his inspirational authorship last night, and if one credits the number of stories about the hon. member's activities prior to his entry into the house, then he is keeping quite in character. Truly sir, this amendment really says nothing. Let us look at it.
This house is of the opinion that the financial proposals of the government, as set forth in the
The Budget

Mr. Lambert budget presented to this house by the Minister of Finance and contrary to the advance publicity-
I ask, Mr. Speaker, whose advance publicity? That of prognosticators in the press? After all, they have a right to speculate, but that was not advance publicity from the government.
-are restrictive of trade and thoroughly inadequate to expand the production and jobs needed to ensure the growth of the economy, despite the burdens imposed by a fifth consecutive deficit of a record size.
We will talk about deficits a little later, Mr. Speaker, and about the attitude of the Liberal party toward deficits, their attitude since 1958 and what their program since that time has meant in potential expenditure.
And the house believes that for this reason, and because of the general mismanagement of the country's financial affairs, the government is not entitled to the confidence of the elected representatives of the people.
These last few words are very reminiscent of 1958 and for that reason they mean just as much as they did then. My only thought is that obviously this amendment is intended to gain the support of the hon. members of that group which is casting about for a name and for a leader but can quite easily answer to the name of the third party. Not only do the Liberals in this house seek to garner unto themselves the elected representatives of that new party but it would appear that the order may have gone out to do the same at the lower echelon; at least, so the young Liberals would appear to have thought in Toronto last week.
I think the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River deserves a better fate than to fight the cause of such an amendment. His was a curious speech but because my colleague, the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell), has dealt at some length with last Thursday's opener by the opposition financial critic I shall make but one or two short comments. First of all, there was an unseemingly long dredging into the past for items of speeches, for statements, some reported accurately and some otherwise, statements taken out of context, glosses put on statements, excerpts from the red bible. I wonder whether they have the red dean too. How that book has been in evidence. On all of the glosses, the excerpted statements, the hon. member built up a number of men of straw. Oh, he worked hard and tortuously to get these creatures to stand up so as to be identifiable at least, but just as hard he worked to knock them down. To what purpose? To consume the major portion of his speech.
I would say that he neglected most of the really important items in the budget. What of the tariff changes? We had heard the hon.

The Budget-Mr. Lambert member on previous occasions speak at great length about tariffs and yet this time I do not recollect having heard him so speak. As financial critic, surely he would have had a good deal to say about the provisions for dominion-provincial fiscal arrangements. These were concretely stated and were not something intangible like the possible effects of the devaluation of the dollar which has so many indefinables. But then I suppose such a course of action as he took was more in keeping with the Cassandra-like mood of the hon. member the other day.
Surely if he were really interested in the economic welfare of the country he would have dwelled much more on the changes concerning the industrial development bank, for instance. These are two-pronged and are most important, and I intend to discuss them in more detail later.
However, Mr. Speaker, the official financial critic was subsequently followed by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate who gave the first of two speeches in the last four or five days which indicate that the hon. member is finding the session long. I am not going to refer to yesterday's effort, but last Thursday evening's effort was quite a contrast with the reasoned though laboured effort of the opposition's opening critic. There was no intelligent development of argument. It was a resort to invective, to personal vilification of the Minister of Finance and of the Prime Minister. One would say there was smear by innuendo and of course there were exaggerated gestures and language. I do not think the indignation he showed was as synthetic, and certainly was not of the order of that which we often get from his running mate, the hon. member for Essex East.
However, there was one thing he said with which I agree. At one stage the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate gloated that he was not thin-skinned. Well, Mr. Speaker, I will agree that at times he has the hide of a rhinoceros. The other night, however, I believe he displayed other characteristics of that animal, certainly in so far as the intelligence of his speech was concerned. Thursday was a bad day for the hon. member as was indicated earlier by the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Best). "Gutless chicken" will be as long remembered as "Canadian babies".
I thoroughly enjoyed the spectacle of the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer), that coiner of pat phrases. I have had experience of him in last year's committee on defence expenditures. He has not changed a bit. On all and sundry occasions we hear flat assertions from him, relying for their validity on the fact that they are statements by the hon. member. He had a great deal to say

about planning and tried to chide the government for a lack of planning. His remarks were general, I point out, and applied to no particular sector.
This love of planning exhibited by the hon. member for Trinity is touching. He was one of the co-chairmen of that famous January conclave. He was one of the backroom boys, sir, who steered the meetings, the conclusions and resolutions. We know just what the result was. If there was any vestige of planning in what came out of that January meeting of the Liberals then the hon. member for Trinity stands alone in the Liberal party in his great love of planning. Of course, we all remember the Pearson plan of 1958. We recall it rather dimly, mind you, because it lived for two short months and has been buried for the past three years.
The hon. member for Trinity tried to make much about the reduction of taxes. He dug into the past, into 1956 and early 1957 for excerpts of speeches by the Prime Minister. Then, the red book came out. He forgot, though, about the reduction in taxes in late 1957 which were worth about $178 million. There were reductions in the rates of personal income taxes, increases in the exemptions of children. Of course, one can forgive the hon. member for Trinity for forgetting that because he was not here then. Undoubtedly, he has forgotten these minor items as well as the upward revision from $25,000 to $35,000 of corporate profits to which the lower 21 per cent rate applies. If this is not lowering taxes, then I do not know what is.
A great deal was said by the hon. member for Trinity about deficits. This was echoed by other members of the opposition, the hon. member for St. Jean-Iberville-Napierville (Mr. Dupuis) and others. However, they conveniently forgot what their leader said about deficits in 1958. He cheerfully promised tax cuts up to $400 million in addition to the $178 million that the Conservatives had put into force in 1957. What has become of the promise to aid young married couples about which we heard so much? We know that the other day they supported increases in family allowances. What about the plan to bring spring wheat, oats and barley under definite price supports? Wheat was supposed to be $1.50 per bushel in 1957 and 1958. This program would take a lot of money, but the Leader of the Opposition was quite candid about it. He cheerfully accepted the fact that he would have to engage in heavy deficit financing.
I would ask hon. members of the opposition, why all this lately discovered concern about deficit financing by their group? Let us ask

them the cost of that great platform of January, 1961. I have heard the estimate put as low as an additional $1,000 million and as high as $1,600 million. Certainly, though, no Liberal who participated in the production of that famous platform has ever publicly admitted that fact, and certainly not the leaders of the Liberal party. They have not admitted the cost of these programs. Unless they are prepared to increase taxes to meet the cost of these items, they are going to have to engage in deficit financing. If they are not so prepared, then the whole program is a sham to deceive the Canadian people. When one considers the added cost today of the $270 million annually for hospital insurance which the Liberals did not have to face prior to 1957, the Liberal program of last January makes absolute nonsense of the opposition's lamentations about deficits, and even greater nonsense of the plea of hon. members such as the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont (Mr. Deschatelets) for tax cuts across the board. I said earlier that the Liberal party was at sixes and sevens in its reaction to the budget. We have had more than ample proof of this fact, Mr. Speaker.
I should like now to turn briefly to the speech of the leading C.C.F. member, the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier). All I can say is that the part of it in which he made direct reference to the budget beggars all description as to its logic. The hon. member complained about exploratory exemptions, and so forth, which he said led to the reckless expansion of our resource industries in the last few years. I should like to see him come out to Alberta and say that. I challenge him to come out there and say that. I defy him to go to any part of the country in which development programs such as we saw in connection with oil and gas, resulted in economic growth in many sectors of the country and tell that part of the country that we have had reckless expansion.
His lack of logic was illustrated in his next remark when he lauded the higher level of the gross national product in those years. How can he reconcile his two arguments? We have these developments of our resource industries which have contributed, in the main, to the development of the gross national products and will continue to do so. He approves of this increase in the gross national product, but he spent a good deal of his time chiding the government because there had been a decrease in the rate of increase in the gross national product. His logic was completely lacking in this argument.
I did say, sir, that I would refer to the industrial development bank. We have seen a great need in this country for medium and
The Budget-Mr. Lambert long range financing in all types of business enterprise. The banks do a good deal of financing. The Canadian chartered banks have a record for which they have no cause to be ashamed. They certainly have participated to the full in the economic growth of this country. However, by reason of their structure and the limitations of the Bank Act, they cannot engage in this medium and long range financing. There has grown over the years, therefore, some use of the industrial development bank in a limited sector. We will now see that use expand in so far as these facilities are available to industry in this country.
If I might make a gentle suggestion to the Minister of Finance, it would be that the true spirit of the amendments to the Industrial Development Bank Act be carried out in the regulations and that we do not hamper or inhibit the use of the credit facilities under the Industrial Development Bank Act. That is one side of the amendment to the Industrial Development Bank Act. However, there is another side and this is a point on which I am glad to see that the Minister of Finance has acceded to the representations which were made not only by myself but by other hon. members and by various organizations throughout the country.
I refer to the fact that in this country, as the minister indicated as found at page 6647 of Hansard in the second column, on ac-casion problems arise where the principal owners of a firm, be it a family owner or otherwise, are facing or anticipating difficulties in connection with estate taxes. We know of instances in which national firms may be developed through' the enterprise, genius and drive of two or three men; those men provided the key to the success of that firm. They may be all able to insure one another so that if, for some reason, one of them should disappear, they are able to buy in his interest and to maintain it within the firm. They are not obliged to sacrifice in order to deal with estate taxes or to settle with the deceased partner's estate and so on.
But there are instances-and I know of some very difficult ones-in which one of the persons involved is not able to get the insurance. There is no means whereby provision can be made for those funds required to clear up the estate taxes or to purchase the interest of the estate. It is suggested that under the Industrial Development Bank Act the bank may be able to participate in the purchase of the shares and in that way to assist the remaining members of the company to keep it together, so that it will not have to be sold at fire sale prices. Again, there is the case of an individual who anticipates that he is not long for this world and that he is going to have quite a sizeable estate.

The Budget-Mr. Carter I know of one case that was referred to me some time ago by the gentleman concerned. His estate will have to pay a very heavy estate tax, and he does not object to paying it; but in order to raise the cash for that purpose, that business will have to be liquidated possibly at fire sale prices, under forced conditions, to the detriment of the estate and any continuing business interest they may have. Yet, on the other hand, today he has offers from foreign interests to buy his business as a going concern. He can take cash to protect his family and to take care of the estate tax problem. But on the other hand, the loss has been that of Canada because a flourishing business has had to be sold to foreign interests. Here again, if I may make a plea to the Minister of Finance, I would express the hope that the regulations, which will embody the spirit and principle of the Industrial Development Bank Act, will be so fashioned and interpreted that we can get the maximum use of it.
I have not referred in very great detail to the provisions of the budget, Mr. Speaker. The Minister of Finance gave a clear picture of those provisions. Hon. members have copies of all of its provisons. I commend it to them for those features which will give to the people of Canada those necessary incentives to improve the economic climate of this country. It is positive action such as that embodied in this budget which will create the right atmosphere for the people of Canada to go forward and not the carping criticism and denigration which we have heard from far too many members of the opposition. Mr. Speaker, I would commend this budget to hon. members of this house and to the people of Canada.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the budget now under debate presents some very interesting contrasts with previous budgets that have been brought down by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming). The increase in wordiness and the decrease in information have already been commented on by various hon. members. I do not think anything more need be said on that score. However, when we examine this budget in the light of last year's budget we can surely be pardoned if we question the accuracy of the minister's economic forecasts and the competence of this government to manage the financial affairs of our nation.
In March, 1960 the minister told us he was budgeting for a surplus of $12 million. In December, 1960 he came and told us the $12 million surplus had now somehow turned into a $286 million deficit. A few days ago he told us that on March 31 instead of a $286 million deficit we were going to have a $345 million deficit. These figures hardly inspire

confidence in the minister's judgment. I can remember the time, and it is not so many years ago, when the minister rather prided himself on the accuracy of his forecasts. He now seems to have given up completely in despair. He told us that we were moving out of a recession and that, even if there were no changes in the budget proposals, we could expect a three per cent increase in our gross national product. He refused, however, to predict how much extra increase would be brought about by his budget proposals. He has now come to the point where he will not even predict what his deficit will be. He cites a figure of about $650 million to $700 million and provides himself with a comfortable margin of $50 million even on his deficit.
With respect to the competence of this government in managing our national affairs may I say this. This government has produced a deficit every year since it took office. There have been four successive deficits and a fifth deficit of $650 million is predicted for the current year. The result of these deficits has been to add over $2 billion to our public debt and to increase our interest charges to about $800 million, making them now the third highest item of federal expenditure, second only to national defence and national health and welfare, When we consider all these things, we can hardly regard this performance as an example of good national housekeeping.
There can be no disagreement, however, with the objectives of the budget; to get our economy rolling; to create jobs; to lower interest rates; to finance a greater proportion of our industrial expansion with Canadian capital. Everyone will welcome the tax cuts on automobiles and the other measures such as research allowances, exploration and development allowances and the extension of the operations of the industrial development bank. All these will receive, I believe, general approval.
However, when these proposals are viewed in the light of our national problems, problems of unemployment, economic slow down, the problem of underdeveloped areas and our unfavourable balance of international accounts, then there is room for a great deal of doubt both as to their adequacy and their effectiveness.
Here, Mr. Speaker, I must record my personal disappointment that apart from the extension of the operations of the industrial development bank this budget contains nothing whatever to stimulate the economy of the Atlantic provinces-

I was saying, Mr. Speaker, that my constituents will be particularly disappointed that apart from putting net making machinery on the free entry list, bringing it down from the most favoured nation tariffs, which means a reduction of only 5 per cent, there is nothing whatever in this budget to assist the fishing industry.
I wish to refer to the recommendations of the Fisheries Council of Canada. Here I am going to read quite extensively from my notes, Mr. Speaker. I am going to read the recommendations of the fisheries council from notes rather than from the letter which I have here. It is more convenient and I think I will save time by following this procedure. The recommendations of the Fisheries Council of Canada that free entry under item 682 be extended to include trawl doors, inflatable life rafts, aluminum fish boxes and pen boards, cordage with metal strands, salt fish dryers and parts, and electrical generating equipment have been completely ignored. Even their request that the 15 per cent duty on anchors weighing under 40 pounds should not apply to commercial fishermen has been refused.
It is doubtful whether the depreciation of the value of the Canadian dollar will be of very much benefit to fishermen. It is true that it will make fish exporters more competitive, but the New England fishermen are already complaining that our fish products are too competitive in their market. While it may tend to increase profits of fish exporters, there is no guarantee whatever that this increase in profits will be passed on to the fishermen in terms of higher prices. On the other hand, their cost of living will rise, and rise substantially. As other hon. members have already pointed out today, not only will their cost of living increase, but their cost of production will also increase because most of the equipment that the fisherman uses, in my province at least, has to be imported.
In view of the risks involved in using the exchange stabilization fund to depreciate the value of our Canadian dollar there is great room for doubting even the wisdom of this proposal. The most heartening thing about the present budget is that the minister has at least conceded that our Canadian economy

The Budget-Mr. Carter is sick. However in this budget, as in previous budgets, the minister seems to have overlooked two very important factors. These are that no matter how accurately he has diagnosed our economic ills, and no matter how good the remedies he has prescribed, there are still two things necessary to make them effective. These two things are the intelligent co-operation of the people and the confidence of the public, particularly of the business community.
The minister cannot expect to get the intelligent co-operation of the people if they do not understand what is required of them and why. I want to suggest to the minister that the wordiness of his budget tends to defeat these two very desirable and necessary ends. If a person comes to me and spends 20 minutes saying something that could be said in five minutes, that certainly does not inspire my confidence in him.

speechtext: The hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) a few moments ago-was not the minister listening to his own colleague? -was decrying the Liberals for all the deficits we were proposing in our resolutions.
