subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And you were complaining about the deficits.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I want to recall to the minister what the hon. member for Edmonton West said. He said the Liberal leader came out and asked for a deficit of $400 million. That was a terrible thing. Here we have the minister telling us that last year he had a deficit of $350 million which was not planned

at all. Not content with that, he comes before us and tells us he is going to have another deficit of $650 million or $700 million this time, and that is not planned either. I am going to prove to the minister just how little planning there is in this budget, but before I go on I just want to answer another thing that the hon. member for Edmonton West said. He went on to say that we have to find $298 million for the hospital insurance plan; the Liberals never had to face anything like that. I want to tell him that as far back as 1957 we had $89 million in the budget for this contingency. So at the time when we were in the depths of a recession the minister steadfastly rejected any suggestion that he should budget for a planned deficit but now that we are on the way out of it he suddenly espouses this cause and becomes alive to its merits. Why has the minister changed his mind? Surely the people are entitled to know. Is it because he has tried everything else and has come to this as a last resource?
I want to tell the minister that it is open to serious doubt whether he has in fact presented us with a planned deficit. The minister has said this is an expansionist budget and I think everybody would agree that if the economy is moving upwards a little more momentum would be all to the good and it would not be a good thing to try to slow it down before it really got under way. We want it to get enough momentum to keep on going. On the other hand we do not want it to get out of control. It might be good politics on the part of the minister to talk about an expansionist budget when the economy is moving upwards, because if the economy is moving up we are going to have expansion anyway. The minister has told us to expect a 3 per cent expansion apart from any effect brought about by his proposals. Will the minister take credit for all the expansion that occurs next year, or only for the expansion that occurs in excess of 3 per cent? I want to tell the minister that there is not much expansion indicated in this white paper which is entitled "Private and Public Investment in Canada Outlook for 1961". If this is really an expansionist budget, how much expansion does it represent? To be healthy, our Canadian economy needs to expand at the rate of at least 6 per cent-2 per cent to take care of the national increase in the working force, another 2 per cent to take care of the backlog of unemployment and a further 2 per cent to provide capital for reinvestment and improvement and to raise our standard of living. Do we have a deficit that is planned to accomplish this? If so, how is it to be achieved? It is certainly not clear from what the minister has told us so far.
The Budget-Mr. Carter
A planned deficit, as I understand it, has two components. One component is designed to put extra purchasing power into the hands of the people and the other is to carry out planned projects. The minister told us when he brought down his budget that his proposals would put only $100 million extra purchasing power into the hands of the people in the whole year, and that for the balance of this year they would receive only $65 million extra spending money. Well, I submit that that is not going to have very much impact on the economy. What about the rest of the budget? What about the rest of the deficit? Last year we had a deficit of $350 million and that was totally unplanned and totally unexpected. Now we are going to have $650 million-$300 million more. To what plans are that extra $300 million deficit geared? The minister has not told us. But the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson) has suggested that it is geared to the spending program which was approved eight months ago. If that is so, and it seems very likely that it is, then it is not related to any expansion project at all.
Another vital question which has been left unanswered is this. What is behind the minister's sudden conversion in favour of using the exchange stabilization fund? Last year he told us it was too dangerous even to contemplate. What is the difference now? He has not told us that.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader

speechtext: Gigantic speculation.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We know that the cost of living will go up, but in addition what will be the cost to the treasury to bring our Canadian dollar down, and not only to bring it down, but to keep it down particularly in the face of the United States dollar which may tend to get stronger on the world market? Where will this money come from? Will we borrow this money or will we just print it, and how will this affect the deficit? In fact, is $650 million a realistic deficit and, if not, how will it affect our cash requirements?
If, as the minister has told us, he already will need $1 billion, if our cash requirement will be $1 billion and if in addition to that we have to borrow more money for the industrial development bank and for the exchange stabilization fund, will that not defeat the minister's efforts to keep interest rates down? Surely that will have the effect of an upward push of interest rates.
Then again what will be the effect of a devalued dollar on other sectors of government spending, for example, in regard to the armed forces? I have an article before me which appeared in the Ottawa Journal on June 24, 1961 headed "Canadian Troops



The Budget-Mr. Rouleau Ask Pay Boost" and bears the date line, "Soest, Germany". Part of this article reads as follows:
Until about a year ago here Canadians received approximately 41 marks on the dollar, give or take a tew "phennings" (100 to a mark or the German equivalent of our cent).
Since then, however, the value of the dollar has dropped 15 per cent, 7.5 per cent of this since mid-January this year, taking in the March revaluation of the Deutschmark.
On the basis of $100 you used to receive 440 marks; now you only get 384, or 57 marks less, equivalent to- a loss of about $15.
A later paragraph of the same article reads as follows:
Sometime this fall the strengthened Deutschmark is to be revalued again. And the question asked is: "If the Canadian dollar is only worth 3.75 now, what's it going to be worth then?"
We might very well ask what it will be worth after the minister has devalued it.
These are all very important questions. I should like to suggest to the minister that the success of his budget proposals will be in direct proportion to the confidence he can inspire in the business community. Businessmen are not interested in the political aspects of the budget and will not be fooled by changes made for political purposes without economic justification. Their confidence will depend on to what extent and with what forthrightness the minister provides the answers to these important questions.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened a few moments ago to the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot (Mr. Ricard) who had risen to take part in the discussion of the budget. The hon. member said that he had no intention of taking part in this debate, but that, in view of the lack of sincerity, or of the "insincerity" of the Liberals, to use his own words, he had decided to do so.
Mr. Speaker, I am asking you, is it a lack of sincerity on the part of the members of the Liberal opposition to take up the case of the unemployed in this country? Is it a lack of sincerity, Mr. Speaker, to defend the businessmen who are having trouble since the Conservatives took over in this country? Is it insincere on the part of the Liberal opposition to make an appeal on behalf of businessmen in Canada? Is the Liberal opposition lacking in sincerity because it wants to defend the Canadian workers and taxpayers? Is it a lack of sincerity, Mr. Speaker, for members of Her Majesty's official opposition to try to co-operate in the restoration of full employment in Canada, in the restoration of prosperity and of the finances of the state?

Mr. Speaker, who is guilty of insincerity, if I may use the expression of the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot? Certainly it is those who, in 1957 and 1958, made irresponsible promises. They were guilty of insincerity in failing to provide to the Canadian people what they had been used to receive during the 22 years of Liberal government.
The hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot managed to pull another neat trick tonight. In taking part in the budget debate, he managed to say not a single word on the budget itself. That shows what the member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot really thinks of the budget speech delivered to us by the Minister of Finance. The hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot suggests that we, of the Liberal opposition, are glad to see the unemployment insurance fund depleted. Well, Mr. Speaker, nothing could be more untrue. What we complain about however, we, Liberal members, is that the unemployment insurance fund that we had succeeded in setting up during our administration, because we were able to ensure full employment, is seriously threatened by the bad administration of the Conservative government which is directly responsible for the present unemployment in our country. But before long, Mr. Speaker, it will be those who sit on this side of the house who will have the responsibility of replenishing that fund, as we did in the past, by restoring prosperity and full employment in Canada.
The hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot stated here tonight in front of his colleagues, that we, on this side of the house are glad that there is unemployment in Canada. Well. As a young Canadian, as a Liberal, as a politician, I take objection to the statement of the member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot. As a Canadian who loves his country and his fellow-citizens, regardless of party affiliations, I cannot rejoice that there should be so much unemployment in our country. As a Liberal, as a member of Her Majesty's loyal opposition, nothing would please me more than if unemployment were on the way out and if all those who suffer at present could find the jobs to which they are entitled and which would enable them to earn their living and benefit from the natural resources with which providence has endowed our country.
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot asserts that all we want on this side of the house is to get back into power.

After four years of Conservative administration, after having travelled here and there in the country and having heard Canadian citizens from all classes complaining, I should say that it is less a case of Liberals wanting to get back into power than a case of the Canadian people being anxious to get rid of a government in which they put their trust in 1957, but which they do not trust any more and which they would gladly replace by one having shown its mettle, namely a Liberal administration.
The member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot told us that we wanted to get back into power only for the sake of being in power. The hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot would do well to read again the report of the Conservative convention held in Ottawa in 1957 when the young Progressive Conservatives were stating that in order to take hold of power in Ottawa they only had to mobilize all the discontented Liberals.
Mr. Tom Bell, then president of the young Conservatives stated:
We are going strong, united and anxious to do a job for our party, and the easiest way to do that is to turn against the Liberals.
Such was the program that the young Conservatives held before the Canadian population.
Well, on this side of the house, we have a concrete program to offer. We have concrete proposals to submit to the people, as we have done during the present session. Unfortunately, those members opposite did not want to listen to us, nor take into account the suggestions we made, so that their administration has put us in a sad plight.
Mr. Speaker, the member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot is not usually so vocal. Perhaps it is the presence here tonight of the candidate to the leadership of the Union Nationale party, Mr. Daniel Johnson, that inspires him. That explains perhaps the severe attitude of the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot.
Mr. Speaker, let us come back to more serious matters. Our political institutions, like our parliamentary traditions, favour a system of political parties representing various shades of opinion.
A certain group, known under the name of Conservatives, accept men and institutions as they are. It is the present Prime Minister who gave that definition of the Conservative party. In practice, that party has shown some preference for restrictive and protectionist policies and a certain leaning toward financial interests which it seeked to protect.
Another group, the extreme left group, known as the C.C.F., advocates a radical evolution in our institutions, including nationalization of production.
The Budget-Mr. Rouleau
The middle of the road party is the Liberal party, which believes that reforms are always required because it is always necessary to adapt oneself to changing conditions in these modern times.
The Liberal party wants to protect the average citizen; it does not want changes as radical as those advocated by the socialists, because it believes that free enterprise is of great service to the nation. But it wants to ensure a more equitable distribution of the wealth of the nation and the fruits of production through social security measures and reforms it has always advocated.
These three schools of thought are constantly opposed in Canada but more particularly in the House of Commons where the elected representatives of the nation meet.
If it falls to the party with the largest number of representatives to govern, to administer the nation's business, the opposition which represents a large proportion of Canadian citizens, has the duty to criticize, and criticize severely when needed, the government measures. The opposition has the duty to point out the faults and omissions of the government, to make observations and suggestions and, let us admit it frankly, to show the nation, the Canadians, the shareholders of this country, that it is more capable of running the country than the government of the day.
In their respective fields, the government, and the opposition, must never forget their responsibility, which is the welfare of the nation and the sound management of the affairs of the country, coming first, before the promotion of a political party.
The government must never make use of its majority in the house to stifle the opposition. It must listen to opposition members with attention and sometimes, let us admit it, with patience.
Opinions are certainly different as to the policy to be followed in order to bring about the general weal. This is something we must never forget in our discussions, but we must take for granted and for sacred the fact that the public weal is the sole care of every member of this house. Any member who does not entertain such an ideal would not deserve to sit in this house.
The system of government we have in Canada encourages such an ideal and I, for one, am convinced that we have now an ideal system of democratic government of which I am proud to be a member and I am grateful to the voters of the Dollard constituency for giving me the opportunity on their behalf to take part in that government.

The Budget-Mr. Rouleau
It is with this preamble as a background that I rise tonight to take part in this debate on the budget.
I wish a greater number of my colleagues of the ministry had participated in this debate, but I find that they, who are usually so loquacious, especially during the present session, when they continuously rose to talk about the most trivial matters, to praise this or that minister, to shower flattery upon the government on all occasions, have become hesitating when it comes to deal with one of the most important measures, if not the most important of all the reasons why we are here, that is the Canadian budget which will directly affect, during the next 12 months and even during years to come, the life of every family, of every Canadian citizen, and which will also affect our relations with every nation of the world.
Our hon. friends opposite, after the applause of the budget night has faded away, are somewhat stunned. They are as quiet as frightened partridges. You would think they are ready, like panic-stricken ostriches, to hide their heads in the sand.
It is no wonder that they are afraid. They have reason to fear not only the anger of their constituents, in view of the complete failure of four years of Conservative administration, but also the worst for the Canadian economy, because of the tremendous gamble the Minister of Finance is taking in his budget. No one can say where we are headed. The experience of the past four years has taught us to fear the worst.

Four years of Conservative administration have given us the following result: five deficits in four years; an increase of $2 billion in the national debt; corresponding increase in the interest on the debt; deterioration of our commercial relations throughout the world; deterioration of our relations with our American neighbours; irreparable deterioration, in some cases, of relations between the government and senior officials, as well as various government agencies.
The Minister of Finance has announced an expansionist budget; indeed the budget is expansionist, but in its deficit.
Last year, he forecast a $12 million surplus and ended up with a deficit of some $345 million. This year, he predicts a deficit ranging between $600 and $700 million. What will be the situation next year?
The policies of the Conservative government have resulted in unenviable records, record deficits, record unemployment, record increase in the interest on the debt in peacetime, and record hesitation, contradiction, incompetence and irresponsibility.
Mr. Speaker, may I call it 10.30?

maintopic: DUMPING OP WASTE, GEORGIA GULF AND BURRARD INLET
DUMPING OP WASTE, GEORGIA GULF AND BURRARD INLET
speechtext:
1.	Have there been any complaints directed to the Department of Transport about the dumping of waste in the gulf of Georgia or Burrard inlet within the last six months?
2.	Has the Department of Transport issued any instructions recently to owners of vessels in the gulf of Georgia or in Burrard inlet with respect to the dumping of refuse in the waters?
3.	Are there any penalties for dumping waste?
4.	Has any action been taken by the Department of Transport to eliminate the nuisance caused by such dumping by owners of vessels?
5.	Has there been an increase in waste dumpage in recent months in Vancouver harbour?
6.	If so, has there been an increase in the staff and equipment of the national harbours board to cope with the situation?
Answer by: Hon. Leon Balcer (Minister of
Transport):
The responsibility of the Department of Transport for the prevention of dumping of
Question
waste or refuse in navigable waters is confined to oil pollution by ships. Within this area of responsibility, the answers to the questions are as follows:
1.	No complaints have been received concerning the discharge of oil in the gulf of Georgia or Burrard inlet within six months.
2.	Vessels are boarded by department inspectors in Vancouver for the purposes of examining oil record books. Public notices are also posted warning of the penalties for discharge of oil into Canadian waters and pilots bringing vessels into west coast Canadian ports are provided with cards advising the master of the ship of the penalties for discharge of oil.
3.	Section 495A of the Canada Shipping Act provides for a penalty of up to $500, and/ or six months' imprisonment.
4.	Surveillance of vessels on a continuous basis is not possible but arrangements have been made with the masters of Canadian government ships and the masters of fisheries inspection vessels to report any cases of oil pollution which come to their attention.
5.	No increase in oil pollution in Vancouver harbour has been reported.
6.	Not applicable.

subtopic: JOINT COMMUNIQUE BY PRIME MINISTERS OF JAPAN AND CANADA

speechtext:
June 26, 1961.
The Prime Minister ol Japan, Hon. Hayato Ikeda, has concluded today a visit to Ottawa made at the invitation of the Prime Minister of Canada, Right Hon. John G. Diefenbaker. Prime Minister Ikeda was accompanied by the foreign minister of Japan, Hon. Zentaro Kosaka, and a number of officials of the government of Japan.
Prime Minister Diefenbaker and Prime Minister Ikeda, together with the Secretary of State for External Affairs, Hon. Howard C. Green, and the Japanese foreign minister, exchanged views on a number of international problems of mutual interest and concern and on questions affecting the relations between Canada and Japan.
They examined the state of east-west relations, with particular attention to recent developments in the Far East. They agreed on the need for a genuinely independent and neutral Laos and on the importance of economic co-operation with the less fully developed nations of Asia. They further exchanged views on communist China.
Prime Minister Ikeda and Prime Minister Diefenbaker welcomed the continuing cooperation of the Canadian and Japanese delegations to the United Nations. They emphasized that they looked forward to even closer co-operation in the future.
The two Prime Ministers also reviewed economic relations between Canada and Japan. Prime Minister Ikeda reaffirmed the principle of orderly marketing of Japanese exports
to Canada of products competitive with Canadian production in order to avoid injury to Canadian industries. Prime Minister Diefenbaker confirmed that the government of Canada looked forward to the continued expansion of mutually beneficial trade between the two countries.
Prime Minister Diefenbaker noted the Japanese interest in the possible establishment and development of Japanese investments in Canada and indicated that mutually satisfactory arrangements would be made for the entry to Canada of Japanese nationals required in connection with certain of the operations of these enterprises. Prime Minister Ikeda explained his government's plans for further liberalization of imports, including commodities of interest to Canada.
The two Prime Ministers agreed that in view of the increasing importance of Canadian-Japanese relations, there should be established a Canadian-Japanese ministerial committee which would not be a negotiating body but would provide a valuable means of contact between ministers of the two countries. The activities of the committee would consist primarily of visits of ministers to each other's country from time to time to exchange views on matters of common interest particularly in the economic field, and to familiarize themselves with the problems of the other country.
At the close of their discussions Prime Minister Ikeda renewed the invitation to Prime Minister Diefenbaker to visit Japan. Prime Minister Diefenbaker accepted this invitation to visit Japan at a mutually convenient time in the near future.
Wednesday, June 28, 1961
